url: /botmux/en/adopt.md
---

import video_v3_adopt_relay_en from '../../static/img/video-v3-adopt-relay-en.mp4';

# Session Adopt

Your CLI is halfway through a task and you have to leave? Send `/adopt` in Lark to bring that **already-running** CLI into the current topic: watch progress and keep sending messages from your phone, and find everything unchanged when you're back at your desk.

Supported terminals: **tmux, Zellij, Herdr, and Orca (experimental)**. The same card also lists **past sessions** of the bot's CLI, so you can resume one into the current topic.

<video src={video_v3_adopt_relay_en} controls preload="metadata" style={{width:'100%',borderRadius:'8px'}} />

## Quick start

1. Start your CLI (for example, Claude Code) as usual in tmux / Zellij / Herdr on your machine.
2. In Lark, send `/adopt` to a **bot bound to the same CLI**.
3. A "📡 Choose a CLI session to adopt" card appears: tap a session to select it, then tap the confirm button below.
4. After "📡 Adopted …", messages you send in the topic are typed straight into that terminal, and the terminal's output and answers sync back to Lark.

To skip the card, name the target directly:

```
/adopt                 # Scan and show the selection card
/adopt 0:2.0           # Adopt a tmux pane (session:window.pane)
/adopt mysess:3        # Adopt a Zellij pane (session:paneId, or session/paneId)
/adopt <Herdr pane ID> # Adopt a Herdr pane
/adopt orca:term_xxx   # Adopt an Orca terminal (experimental)
/adopt <session ID>    # Resume a past session (the CLI's own session ID)
```

## What's on the selection card

The card mixes two kinds of candidates and supports search (title / project / path) and paging:

| Source | What it is | Confirm button | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 🟢 Running | A local CLI **currently running** in tmux / Zellij / Herdr / Orca | Take over into this topic | Bridged to the original terminal; the process keeps running |
| 🕘 History | A session of the same CLI saved on disk that can be resumed | Resume into this topic | Botmux relaunches the CLI with `--resume`; it becomes a normal Botmux session |

Each candidate shows the CLI, path, uptime (or last activity), and "Location". For tmux, Zellij, and Herdr the heading is the workspace or tab name and "Location" holds the session / pane locator; Orca headings use the terminal or CLI session title.

Filtering rules:

* **Only the bot's own CLI is listed**: a Pi bot won't list Codex or TRAE panes, so the CLI behind the bot never changes silently.
* **Botmux's own sessions are hidden**: persistent `bmx-*` sessions and any session Botmux already manages (open or closed) are excluded. To bring back a Botmux session you closed, use "Resume session" on its session card.
* **A running session never shows up again under History.**
* **History lists at most the 20 most recent sessions.** Use search to narrow it down, or run `/adopt <session ID>` directly.
* **Only the person who summoned the card can use it.** Others should send their own `/adopt`.

CLIs that support History: Claude Code, Codex, TRAE CLI, Grok, OpenCode / OpenCode 2, Antigravity, Genius. For other CLIs the card shows live sessions only.

## After adopting: a bridge, not a takeover

When you adopt a live session, Botmux only observes and writes input to the target terminal. It **never changes the original terminal's focus, layout, or size**.

* **Both sides stay in sync**: messages from Lark are typed into the terminal, and terminal output appears on the streaming card in real time. On adoption you first get a "📜 Last exchange before /adopt" card so you know where things stand; anything you type directly in the terminal also syncs to Lark as a "🖥️ Local terminal turn".
* **Disconnect any time**: tap "⏏ Disconnect" on the streaming card, or send `/detach` (alias `/disconnect`; `/close` in an adopted topic does the same). Botmux removes only its own side and **never ends your CLI**; the original process keeps running locally.
* **One adopted session per topic**: sending `/adopt` again in a topic that already has one asks you to disconnect first.

> The old "🔄 Take Over" button is retired: new cards don't show it, and tapping it on an old card does nothing. Today adopt has a single form, the shared bridge.

## Resuming a past session

Pick a "🕘 History" entry on the card, or send `/adopt <session ID>`. Botmux relaunches the CLI with `--resume` in the original working directory and picks up that conversation. Unlike the bridge, **Botmux now starts and manages the CLI**, just like any new session (it can be restarted, and closing it ends the process).

If the ID belongs to a Botmux session:

* In the **current topic** → it's resumed directly.
* In **another topic** → it isn't moved here. You're asked to tap "Resume session" in the original topic, or run `botmux resume <id>` locally.

## Notes for Codex users

**Drafts are never overwritten.** If the adopted Codex terminal has an unsubmitted local draft, Botmux keeps the draft, doesn't append the Lark message, and asks you to submit or clear it in the terminal before resending. Orca terminals behave the same way, and Botmux also stops if it can't reach Orca to confirm the composer is empty.

**When Codex uses a shared background server**, Botmux still types into the original tmux pane. We recommend enabling `thread-id` (legacy name `session-id`) in Codex's `/statusline` and keeping the full ID visible. Botmux uses it to confirm which session received your message and to follow `/new` or `/resume` switches you make in the terminal.

**Codex App conversations.** If the bot's CLI is `codex-app`, `/adopt` lists existing Codex App conversations instead ("📱 Choose a Codex App conversation"). Pick one to continue that thread in the topic, or send `/adopt <threadId>` (an ID prefix works too).

**Sharing a Codex App on your dev machine (experimental).** To have Lark and the desktop Codex App connected to the **same** App Server and the same thread at once, add this to a bot whose `cliId` is `codex` or `codex-app`:

```json
{
  "existingAppServer": { "endpoint": "unix:///absolute/path/app-server.sock" }
}
```

`endpoint` accepts local addresses only: a `unix://` socket with an absolute path, or `ws://127.0.0.1:<port>`. Then pick a conversation with `/adopt` to share it. Botmux never creates or stops the App Server; `/detach` disconnects only the Lark side, and the App Server and Codex App session keep running. Avoid submitting different tasks from both sides at the same time. If the remote terminal shows "Hooks need review" the first time, choose "Continue without trusting" in the Web Terminal; Botmux won't trust all hooks for you. This mode can't be combined with `codexBrowser`, `codexRpcInput`, or `wrapperCli`.

## Orca (experimental)

Orca works in two modes:

* **Server mode**: a persistent orcad on Linux, with its CLI at `~/.orca/cli/bin/orca`.
* **SSH relay mode**: when Botmux and the SSH terminal run on the **same** Linux host, Botmux connects directly to the local relay that owns the original PTY. This route doesn't need the desktop client, so you can close your Mac and still send `/adopt` to get back to the session. **Cross-host** relays still go through the desktop, which must stay online.

Things to know:

* Before adopting, Botmux checks the terminal's identity (handle, PTY incarnation, workspace, local process ownership). Terminals without a stable identity are neither listed nor restored, so a reused terminal handle can't receive your input. Older relays without incarnation data can't use the direct route.
* Sessions previously adopted through the desktop relay need one more `/adopt` to switch to the direct local route.
* The Web Terminal shows a text screen: you can view and type, but source colors, exact cursor state, and mouse modes aren't kept. After the desktop disconnects, the screen is rebuilt from retained output; if that output starts in the middle of a redraw, the screen may be incomplete.
* Orca/relay versions, terminal redraw behavior, and each CLI's transcript format affect compatibility. If sessions stop being listed, or the screen or replies look wrong after an upgrade, adopt again and report your version details.

## What each CLI gets

| CLI | What works |
|---|---|
| Claude Code, Codex, TRAE | Terminal I/O + structured replies + scrollable history rebuilt from the transcript |
| MTR, Hermes, and other unverified CLIs | Basic terminal access only: live screen, Lark input, and Web Terminal work; structured replies and scrollable history aren't guaranteed |

The last row isn't a terminal I/O limitation. Botmux simply can't reliably prove which transcript belongs to that terminal: MTR can't tell sessions apart when several share one directory, and an externally started Hermes session has no Botmux session marker. Botmux won't guess from "the newest session in the same directory", because that could send another terminal's conversation to Lark.

## Limits

An adopted process runs **on your machine** and its lifecycle isn't Botmux's to manage, so these boundaries apply:

| Action | Result |
|---|---|
| `/relay` to another group | Not supported. To continue elsewhere, start a new session and hand off |
| Fork, restart, or resume an adopted session | Not supported; Botmux won't touch your tmux pane or CLI process |
| The CLI exits on its own | The session ends with it ("⏏ Adopted CLI session has exited.") and isn't relaunched |
| `/adopt` on a bot with the file sandbox on | Rejected. A sandbox can only be applied at launch, not wrapped around a running process; sending a message instead starts a new sandboxed session |
| The topic is waiting for you to pick a repo | Tap "Close session" on the card first, then `/adopt` again |
| `/dismiss` while the group has an adopted session | The group isn't disbanded. `/detach` in that topic first, then `/dismiss` |

After a daemon restart, Botmux first checks whether the adopted CLI is still there:

* Confirmed gone → the session is closed.
* Still running → it's reattached automatically, without posting a recovery card.
* Can't tell right now (for example, a transient probe failure) → the session isn't closed, but it's held without reattaching. It's checked again on the **next daemon restart**, not automatically when your next message arrives.

## Typical usage

Claude Code is running in tmux on your office computer and you have to leave: send `/adopt` from Lark on your phone → pick the session → confirm, and it syncs right away. Keep watching and sending on the road; back at your desk, tap "⏏ Disconnect" and carry on in the terminal. It's not remote control; it's one session shared across devices.

Related pages: [Slash commands](/botmux/en/slash-commands.md), [Relay](/botmux/en/relay.md), [File sandbox](/botmux/en/sandbox.md), [tmux](/botmux/en/tmux.md).



---
url: /botmux/en/api-core-only.md
---

# Core-only (apiOnly) API Control

> Want to embed botmux in your own system and drive a CLI over HTTP, without touching Feishu? Use core-only.
>
> It is botmux as **one process, on a fixed port, listening only on `127.0.0.1`**: no Feishu credentials, no `bots.json`, no supervisor or dashboard. Your orchestrator (task runner, CI, backend service, sandbox) asks it over HTTP to run a CLI (codex / claude-code / …), polls the result, and opens a web terminal when it needs to see what's happening.

This page is for integrators **embedding botmux into their own product**, for example a botmux inside a sandbox running codex.

If you only want an external system to trigger a **normal bot already running in a Feishu group**, see [Triggering Tasks via API](/botmux/en/api-task-trigger.md). The two pages complement each other: the request body, idempotency and polling states work exactly the same under core-only. This page only covers what's specific to core-only: startup, readiness, interrupting a turn, the web terminal, auth, and the security boundary.

Two related entry points: to start sessions and fetch results from a local script or CI, use [Headless Automation Sessions](/botmux/en/headless-session.md); to let OpenAI-protocol tools reuse a CLI's model login, use [Model Proxy](/botmux/en/model-proxy.md) (it runs a core-only instance underneath).

***

## At a glance

```
Your orchestrator                         botmux serve --api-only (127.0.0.1:8930)
─────────────────                         ─────────────────────────────────────────
1. Start the process, wait for       ──▶  bind port → restore old sessions → print ready line
   GET /healthz → 200
2. POST /api/trigger (async)         ──▶  start the CLI (codex / claude-code …) on the task
                                     ◀──  { sessionId, triggerId }
3. GET  …/trigger-result (poll)      ──▶  running → completed / failed / interrupted
   (optional) POST …/turns/<triggerId>/interrupt  stop only this turn, keep the session
4. (optional) GET …/write-link       ──▶  returns an interactive web terminal URL
   (signed)
```

A typical integration only needs steps 1–3, and none of them require signing.

***

## 1. How it differs from normal botmux

| | `botmux start` (fleet) | `botmux serve --api-only` (core-only) |
|---|---|---|
| Processes | supervisor + dashboard + one daemon per bot | **one process**, in the foreground; the service lives as long as the process |
| Feishu credentials | `larkAppSecret` required | **not needed at all**; never connects to Feishu |
| Bot config | `~/.botmux/bots.json` / `BOTS_CONFIG` | **ignores both**; generates exactly one apiOnly bot (still reads the global `~/.botmux/.env` and global config) |
| Where results go | replies posted to a Feishu topic | **nothing is sent to Feishu**; results are only available over HTTP |
| Port | probes upward if taken | fixed port, `127.0.0.1` only, **exits if it can't bind** |
| Data directory | `~/.botmux/data` | its own `~/.botmux/core-only/<botId>/data` |

In one line: core-only is a **headless, single-tenant, loopback-only** botmux. It keeps the full daemon HTTP interface and just drops the Feishu side.

***

## 2. Startup

```bash
# Recommended: the CLI subcommand. Runs in the foreground and inherits stdout,
# so your launcher can watch for the ready line
BOTMUX_API_PORT=8930 botmux serve --api-only

# Same thing with flags
botmux serve --api-only --port 8930 --cli codex --working-dir /path/to/repo

# With an npm install you can also run the entry file directly (for embedded spawn;
# the single-file binary has no dist/, so use the subcommand above)
BOTMUX_API_PORT=8930 node <pkg>/dist/index-core-only.js
```

Flags and env vars (a flag wins when both are given):

| Flag | Env var | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--port` | `BOTMUX_API_PORT` | none, **required** | Listen port; exits if it can't bind |
| `--bot` | `BOTMUX_API_ONLY_BOT` | `local_riff` | Bot id; must look like `local_<name>` (letters, digits, `.`, `_`, `-`) |
| `--cli` | `BOTMUX_CORE_CLI` | `codex-app` | Which CLI to run, e.g. `codex`, `claude-code` |
| `--working-dir` | `BOTMUX_CORE_WORKING_DIR` | current directory | The CLI's working directory |
| `--state-dir` | `BOTMUX_CORE_STATE_DIR` | `~/.botmux/core-only/<botId>/data` | Where session data lives |
| `--backend` | `BOTMUX_CORE_BACKEND` | `tmux` | `tmux` or `pty`. Pick `pty` only if the host can't run a reliable tmux server; with `pty` the terminal can't be reattached after a daemon restart |
| none | `BOTMUX_CORE_MODEL` | unset | Override the default model |
| none | `BOTMUX_CORE_CODEX_AUTH_SYNC` | unset (shared) | Set to `isolated` to make Codex use only this bot's own `CODEX_HOME`, never reading or copying the machine's global login |

**Which CLI?**

* `codex-app` (default): runs through the app-server, returns structured results, **no visible terminal**.
* `codex`, `claude-code`, etc.: run the real TUI in tmux, which you can watch or take over through the web terminal (see section 4).

### When is it "up"?

The daemon **binds the port first, then restores old sessions**. A port that accepts connections isn't ready for tasks yet — wait for readiness:

* **The stdout ready line** (fixed format; match with the regex `^\[core-only\] listening on `), printed only after restore completes:
  ```
  [core-only] listening on 127.0.0.1:8930 (bot local_riff, cli codex-app)
  ```
* **`GET /healthz`** (no signing):
  * not ready → `503 {"ok":false,"status":"starting"}`
  * ready → `200 {"ok":true}`

While not ready, `/api/trigger`, `trigger-result`, `insight`, `host-facts` and the interrupt route also return `503 starting` right away, so even if you skip the probe you can't send a task into a session that is still being restored. Still, the recommended flow is: **poll `/healthz` until 200, then send the first task**.

> `/__health` is public too, but it **always returns 200**. It only tells you the process is alive, not whether it can take tasks.

***

## 3. Running tasks: trigger, poll, interrupt

For the full request body, idempotency keys and polling states, see [Triggering Tasks via API](/botmux/en/api-task-trigger.md). Core-only adds a few rules:

| Rule | Details |
|---|---|
| An HTTP response mode is required | Set `options.waitForFinalOutput` (wait for the result) or `options.asyncReturnSessionId` (get a sessionId back). With neither → `400 bad_request`, since there's no Feishu group to reply into |
| No Feishu targets | A real Feishu `chatId` or `rootMessageId` → `400` |
| You can continue your own session | `target.sessionId` must be one of this service's own sessions; use it to add another turn to the same session |
| The instruction goes in top-level `instruction` | Not `prompt` |
| Poll with the full sessionId | It's a UUID, not the `[worker:xxxxxxxx]` short tag in the logs; the short tag gives `session_not_found` |
| `options.model` / `options.reasoningEffort` | Only apply to CLIs that support switching model / reasoning effort, and only for new sessions; see the trigger docs |

### Trigger and poll

```bash
# Trigger (async): no signing
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8930/api/trigger -X POST -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{
  "source": {"type": "webhook"},
  "target": {"kind": "turn", "botId": "local_riff"},
  "envelope": {"format": "text", "sourceName": "my-runner", "trusted": false},
  "instruction": "Run the tests and report results",
  "options": {"asyncReturnSessionId": true}
}'
# → {"ok":true, "triggerId":"trg_...", "async":{"sessionId":"<uuid>", ...}}

# Poll: no signing
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:8930/api/sessions/<uuid>/trigger-result"
# → state: running / completed / failed / not_found; an interrupted turn is interrupted
```

> Use **v3.9.0 or later**. On older versions, a core-only claude-code first turn could stay `running` forever.

### Stop just this turn (keep the session)

If a task goes off track and you want to stop it but keep the session for more turns, use the interrupt route (no signing):

```bash
curl -s -X POST "http://127.0.0.1:8930/api/sessions/<uuid>/turns/<triggerId>/interrupt"
# → {"ok":true, "action":"interrupted", "sessionId":"<uuid>", "triggerId":"trg_..."}
```

* It only stops **the turn you name**. botmux first confirms the CLI is really running that turn before sending the interrupt; if it can't confirm, it refuses rather than stopping some other turn.
* Polling that turn afterwards returns `state: "interrupted"`. The session stays open, so you can send the next turn with `target.sessionId`.
* Interrupting the same turn again just returns success (with `idempotent: true`).
* Possible failures: `404` (session doesn't exist or is closed, or this session has no such turn), `409` (the turn already finished, isn't running in the current daemon process, or the CLI has already moved past it), `503` (the interrupt wasn't delivered; retry later).

To **close the whole session**, use `POST /api/sessions/:id/close`. It needs signing; see "Close the whole session" in [Triggering Tasks via API](/botmux/en/api-task-trigger.md).

### Reading session-host facts

If you use botmux as a host for CLI sessions and need to know "is this session still there?", read:

```bash
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:8930/api/sessions/<uuid>/host-facts"
```

It returns `{ ok: true, facts: {...} }` with:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `sessionId` / `cli` / `backend` / `sessionStatus` | Session id, CLI, backend (tmux/pty), and whether the session is `active` or `closed` |
| `liveness` | One of `exists` / `missing` / `unknown` |
| `worker.present` / `ready` / `generation` | Whether a worker exists, whether it's ready, and which generation it is |
| `native.sessionId` | The CLI's own session/thread id |
| `native.activeTurnId` | botmux's id for the current turn (not the CLI's internal turn id) |

It **never** returns a tmux socket, PID, worker token, environment variables, or terminal write access.

Two things to keep in mind:

* `unknown` is not `missing`. Don't start a replacement session because of it.
* A CLI turn ending doesn't mean your business task is done. Your orchestrator should still validate the result and save its own evidence before moving its state forward.

***

## 4. Web terminal

With a visible CLI (`--cli codex`, `claude-code`, etc.) you can watch the CLI live in a browser, or even type into it.

### Read-only: already in the poll result

As long as the session's worker is alive, the `trigger-result` response also carries `readOnlyUrl` and `viewToken`. Open `readOnlyUrl` to watch; you can't type.

Once the session is closed, or after a restart before a live worker exists, these fields are left out, so any link you get can actually connect. This is core-only only; a normal fleet's poll response never carries them.

The `viewToken` belongs to the current worker: when the worker restarts it gets a new one and the old link stops working. Use the read-only link from your latest poll; don't cache it long-term.

### Interactive: call `write-link` (signed)

```bash
# write-link needs the section 6 signature headers
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:8930/api/sessions/<sid>/write-link" \
  -H "X-Botmux-Cli-Ts: ..." -H "X-Botmux-Cli-Nonce: ..." -H "X-Botmux-Cli-Auth: ..."
# → {"ok":true, "url":"http://127.0.0.1:<proxyPort>/s/<sid>?token=<write-token>"}
```

* The URL carries a write token; opening it gives you a terminal you can type into. The write token is **only** available here and never appears in poll results.
* Common errors: `401` (bad signature), `404 session_not_active` (session not running), `409 terminal_unavailable` (the worker terminal isn't available right now).

**Fetch the URL each time you "open the terminal", and store only the sessionId.** A session's write token stays the same across worker cycles and daemon restarts, but the port, host and whether the worker is online can change. Fetching is cheap (a local request plus a signature) and always gives you an address that connects.

> A single core-only session isn't reclaimed for being idle (up to 30 live workers by default, and no idle timeout by default), so the terminal normally stays available.

***

## 5. Which routes need signing

Core-only routes come in three layers. **Integrators only need the first**; the other two help you understand the security boundary.

**Layer 1: public routes (no signing)** — only these:

| Route | Method | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `/healthz` | GET | Readiness probe |
| `/api/trigger` | POST | Start a turn |
| `/api/sessions/:id/trigger-result` | GET | Poll the result |
| `/api/sessions/:id/insight` | GET | Poll conversation and progress |
| `/api/sessions/:id/host-facts` | GET | Read session-host facts |
| `/api/sessions/:id/turns/:triggerId/interrupt` | POST | Interrupt only the named turn |

`/__health` is also public in every mode, but it only means the process is alive.

This list is deliberately narrow: other processes on the same machine (including commands the model itself runs) can reach `127.0.0.1` too, so only "drive your own task, read your own result" is open. For example `/api/asks/answer`, which answers an AskUserQuestion, is **not** on the list: it isn't tied to a session, so opening it would let another process answer on your behalf.

**Layer 2: in-session routes (the CLI proves who it is)**. For example `POST /api/session-ready`, `POST /api/asks`, `POST /api/sessions/:id/{slash,cd,close,…}`, `POST /api/hooks/emit`. The caller is the CLI inside the session, using a per-turn rotating credential bound to its session, so it can only act on its own session. Integrators normally don't call these.

**Layer 3: host / operator routes (need the section 6 signature)**. Everything not in the first two layers, e.g. `GET /api/sessions/:id/write-link`, `GET /api/sessions/:id` (session details), `POST /api/sessions/:id/close`.

> `close` is a special case: external callers must sign, and the in-session CLI can also close itself with its layer-2 credential.

***

## 6. How to sign (the usual mistake is the bind)

Signed requests carry three headers:

| Header | Value |
|---|---|
| `X-Botmux-Cli-Ts` | Unix timestamp in **seconds**; allowed skew ±30 seconds |
| `X-Botmux-Cli-Nonce` | Random hex string; must not repeat within 60 seconds |
| `X-Botmux-Cli-Auth` | `HMAC_SHA256(secret, msg)`, encoded as **base64url** |

`secret` is the 43-character base64url text in `~/.botmux/.dashboard-secret`. **Use it as-is as the key; don't base64-decode it first.** The request must come from a loopback address.

`msg` must include the bind, which ties the signature to "method + path + port" so it can't be replayed against another route:

```
bind = `${METHOD} ${pathname} ${port}`     // e.g. "GET /api/sessions/<sid>/write-link 8930"
msg  = `${ts}:${nonce}:${bind}`
```

Three common mistakes:

1. `port` is the port the service **actually listens on** (e.g. `8930`), not the value in the Host header.
2. `pathname` **has no query string** (use `new URL(...).pathname`).
3. `secret` is the raw string; don't decode it.

> If you sign only `ts:nonce` and forget the bind, you get `401 {"reason":"sig_mismatch"}`. Because public routes don't check signatures, this usually shows up **the first time you call write-link**, and it's easy to mistake for a wrong secret or clock. Other `reason` values: `ts_window` (clock off by more than 30 seconds), `replay` (repeated nonce), `missing_headers`.

Reference implementation (same logic as `daemonIpcAuthHeaders()` in `src/core/daemon-ipc-auth.ts`):

```js
import { createHmac, randomBytes } from 'node:crypto';

function coreOnlyAuthHeaders(secret, method, path, port) {
  const pathname = new URL(path, `http://127.0.0.1:${port}`).pathname; // strip the query string
  const ts = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000).toString();
  const nonce = randomBytes(8).toString('hex');
  const bind = `${method.toUpperCase()} ${pathname} ${port}`;
  const sig = createHmac('sha256', secret)          // secret = raw base64url string
    .update(`${ts}:${nonce}:${bind}`)
    .digest('base64url');
  return {
    'X-Botmux-Cli-Ts': ts,
    'X-Botmux-Cli-Nonce': nonce,
    'X-Botmux-Cli-Auth': sig,
  };
}
```

***

## 7. Security boundary

Core-only doesn't talk to Feishu, serves a single tenant, and only uses loopback. Around that, it isolates itself by default:

* **No Feishu**: never creates a Feishu client, and never hands `larkAppSecret` to CLI child processes.
* **No real bot config**: ignores `~/.botmux/bots.json` and removes `BOTS_CONFIG` from the environment, so the CLI can't read other bots' credentials on the same machine.
* **Separate data directory**: session data always lives in `~/.botmux/core-only/<botId>/data` (or your `--state-dir`). An inherited `SESSION_DATA_DIR` from a parent process can't point it at the real fleet's data. The internal signing key used for task reports also lives separately in this directory and is never shared with a fleet on the same machine. (The `~/.botmux/.dashboard-secret` used for section 6 signatures is a different thing.)
* **Local only**: the worker's web server and the advertised terminal address are both fixed to `127.0.0.1`, never exposed on other interfaces.
* **Leaves the host install alone**: no auto-update, auto-restart or `botmux restart`. The `botmux` command wrapper for the CLI goes into `bin/` under its own data directory and never overwrites the machine's `~/.botmux/bin`.
* **Loopback isn't trust**: other processes on the machine (including sandboxes that share the network by default) can also reach `127.0.0.1`, so every route outside layer 1 requires auth.

***

## Appendix: route cheat-sheet

| Route | Method | Auth | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/healthz` | GET | public | Readiness probe (503 starting / 200 ok) |
| `/api/trigger` | POST | public | Start a turn (an HTTP response mode is required) |
| `/api/sessions/:id/trigger-result` | GET | public | Poll the result; carries `readOnlyUrl` + `viewToken` while the worker is alive |
| `/api/sessions/:id/insight` | GET | public | Poll conversation and progress |
| `/api/sessions/:id/host-facts` | GET | public | Session, CLI, backend and liveness |
| `/api/sessions/:id/turns/:triggerId/interrupt` | POST | public | Interrupt only the named turn; the session stays open |
| `/api/sessions/:id/write-link` | GET | **signed** | Interactive web terminal URL (fetch when opening) |
| `/api/sessions/:id` | GET | **signed** | Session details |
| `/api/sessions/:id/close` | POST | **signed**, or the in-session CLI's own credential | Close the session |

For request fields, error codes, what each polling state means and restart behavior, see [Triggering Tasks via API](/botmux/en/api-task-trigger.md).



---
url: /botmux/en/api-task-trigger.md
---

# Trigger botmux Tasks via API

> Want an external system (task orchestrator, CI, backend service…) to hand an instruction to a botmux bot and get the result back programmatically? Use `POST /api/trigger`. The bot runs its CLI as usual; the task can stay entirely out of Feishu, or land in a real group or thread.

This page is for **client developers**. The first three sections cover the common case; the rest is the full reference for fields, status codes and edge cases — look things up as you need them.

***

## 1. Quick start

The most common pattern: **trigger async → poll for the result**, without touching Feishu at all.

**Step 1: get a token.** Run `botmux dashboard`. The part after `?t=` in the printed login URL is your token (see §3).

**Step 2: trigger the task.**

```bash
curl -X POST "http://<daemon-host>:7891/api/trigger" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -H "Cookie: botmux_dashboard_token=$TOKEN" \
  -d '{
    "source":{"type":"webhook"},
    "target":{"kind":"turn","botId":"cli_xxx"},
    "instruction":"Reply with exactly one line: ASYNC_DEMO_OK",
    "envelope":{"format":"json","sourceName":"demo","trusted":false},
    "options":{"asyncReturnSessionId":true}
  }'
```

`botId` is the target bot's Feishu app ID (`larkAppId` in `bots.json`). The response comes back immediately — keep `target.sessionId`:

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "triggerId": "trg_87e7b415-...",
  "action": "queued",
  "target": { "kind": "turn", "sessionId": "2eed60c4-...", "chatId": "http_async_..." },
  "async": { "status": "pending", "sessionId": "2eed60c4-..." }
}
```

**Step 3: poll for the result.**

```bash
curl "http://<daemon-host>:7891/api/sessions/2eed60c4-.../trigger-result" \
  -H "Cookie: botmux_dashboard_token=$TOKEN"
```

Look at `state`: on `running`, check again in a few seconds; on `completed`, the answer is in `output.content`. All states are in §9.

***

## 2. Two decisions: how you get the result, and where it lands

A trigger is defined by two **independent** dimensions. **Whether the task enters a Feishu group is decided only by `target`, not by sync vs async.**

**How you get the result (`options`)**

| Mode | How | HTTP behavior | Pollable | Stoppable |
|------|-----|---------------|:--------:|:---------:|
| **Async** (recommended) | `asyncReturnSessionId: true` | Returns a `sessionId` immediately | ✓ | ✓ |
| **Sync** | `waitForFinalOutput: true` | Holds the connection until output or timeout | — | ✗ |
| **Fire-and-forget** | neither flag | Returns immediately; the answer goes out as a normal Feishu reply | ✗ (see §6.3) | Close the session only |

**Where it lands (`target`)**

| Shape | What to pass | Lands on |
|-------|--------------|----------|
| **Virtual session** | none of `chatId` / `sessionId` / `rootMessageId` | A synthetic session that never enters Feishu |
| **Real group** | `chatId` | A real session in that group |
| **Existing thread** | `chatId` + `rootMessageId` | Appended to that thread |
| **Existing session** | `sessionId` | A new turn on that session |

Common combinations:

| You want to… | Use |
|--------------|-----|
| Run a pure background task with zero Feishu noise | virtual + async (or sync) |
| Drop an event into a group like a webhook and have the answer posted there | real group + fire-and-forget |
| Let the group watch the bot work, but hand the answer to your program | real group + async/sync (⚠️ the group never sees the final answer, see §5.5) |
| Ask follow-ups on the same session | existing session + async, with `turnIdempotencyKey` |

> Hard rule: **if you pass none of the three target fields, you must enable async or sync**, otherwise 400 `target_required` — the task would have neither a Feishu exit nor an HTTP exit.

***

## 3. Authentication

Requests go to the Dashboard (default port `7891`) and use the Dashboard login token:

* **Send the token as a cookie**: `Cookie: botmux_dashboard_token=<TOKEN>`.
* ⚠️ Don't use `?t=<TOKEN>`: that's for browser login. It answers with a **302 redirect** that sets a cookie, so programmatic calls fail.
* Get the token by running `botmux dashboard`. If there's no token yet, it creates one.
* The token stays valid until you run `botmux dashboard rotate` to replace it (the old one stops working immediately).

***

## 4. Request body

```jsonc
{
  "source":   { "type": "webhook" },                  // see 4.1
  "target":   { "kind": "turn", "botId": "cli_xxx" }, // see 4.2
  "instruction": "What you want the bot to do",       // trusted; rendered as the top-level task
  "envelope": {                                        // see 4.3
    "format": "json",
    "sourceName": "your-system",
    "trusted": false                                   // must be false
  },
  "presentation": { "title": "…", "topicMessage": "…" },  // optional, see 4.4
  "options": { /* see 4.5 */ }
}
```

### 4.1 `source`

| Field | Required | Notes |
|-------|:--------:|-------|
| `type` | ✓ | Only `webhook` / `ui` / `workflow` / `schedule` / `vc_meeting` / `headless`; anything else (including typos) is 400 `bad_request` |
| `connectorId` | | Connector ID; used for the default title when `envelope.sourceName` is missing |
| `requestId` | | Your request ID; written to the call log |
| `receivedAt` | | When the upstream received the event |

For ordinary external calls, **always use `"webhook"`**. Only two values change behavior: `headless` (takes the local headless path, see [Headless Automation Sessions](/botmux/en/headless-session.md)) and `vc_meeting` (compact rendering of event content).

### 4.2 `target`

| Field | Required | Notes |
|-------|:--------:|-------|
| `kind` | ✓ | Use `"turn"`. `"workflow"` is retired and returns **410 `legacy_workflow_retired`** |
| `botId` | ✓ | The target bot's `larkAppId`. Missing → 400 `target_required`; doesn't match the target daemon → 400 `bot_not_found` |
| `chatId` | | A real group ID, see §5.2 |
| `sessionId` | | Continue an existing session. Not found → 404 `session_not_found` |
| `rootMessageId` | | Root message ID of an existing thread. Without `sessionId`, **`chatId` is also required** |

### 4.3 `envelope` (external event data, untrusted by default)

| Field | Required | Notes |
|-------|:--------:|-------|
| `sourceName` | ✓ | Your system's name; used for the default title and topic seed |
| `trusted` | ✓ | **Must be literally `false`** |
| `format` | ✓ | Informational; use `"json"` (the daemon doesn't read it) |
| `headers` | | Raw request headers |
| `payload` | | Raw event body |
| `rawText` | | Raw text |

Why `trusted` must be `false`: prompt-injection protection. The daemon wraps the whole envelope as "untrusted external data" and tells the model not to follow instructions hidden inside it. **Put what you actually want the bot to do in the top-level `instruction`** — it's rendered as a trusted task above the event data.

> Exception: when a [Webhook connector](/botmux/en/webhook.md) enables "treat event content as trusted instructions", the Dashboard adds a top-level `payloadTrusted: true` when forwarding (`envelope.trusted` stays `false`), and the event content is rendered as a trusted task. It's only accepted with `source.type: "webhook"` + `target.kind: "turn"`; other combinations get 400. You don't need it when calling this API directly — just put the task in `instruction`.

### 4.4 `presentation` (optional; how it shows up in Feishu)

| Field | Values | Default / notes |
|-------|--------|-----------------|
| `title` | 1–200 chars | Session title (Dashboard / thread name), truncated to 50 chars. Default `[External] <sourceName>` |
| `topicMessage` | 1–200 chars, or `null` | The seed message posted when a new thread is opened. Default `外部事件触发：{sourceName}` ("External event: …"); `null` means no seed |
| `thinking` | `"hidden"` | Hides only this turn's "thinking" bubble; business messages and the HTTP result are unaffected |
| `liveCard` | `"on-start"` | Only for chat-level sessions in regular groups: posts a fresh streaming card once this turn's input is actually handed to the CLI |

* A non-empty explicit `topicMessage` asks for a dedicated thread (except in regular groups in `shared` mode, which keep the shared session).
* `title` and `topicMessage` **only matter when a new thread is opened**: virtual sessions post nothing to Feishu, and existing threads/sessions get no seed.
* Out of range (empty, over 200 chars, wrong type) → 400 `bad_request`.

### 4.5 `options`

**Common fields**

| Field | Validation | Notes |
|-------|------------|-------|
| `asyncReturnSessionId` | boolean | Async mode |
| `waitForFinalOutput` | boolean | Sync mode. Both together → 400 |
| `timeoutMs` | `1000`–`300000` | Sync wait limit, default `120000` (2 minutes) |
| `idempotencyKey` | non-empty, ≤200 chars | Prevent duplicate new sessions, see §8.1 |
| `turnIdempotencyKey` | non-empty, ≤200 chars | Prevent duplicate follow-up turns, see §8.2. Mutually exclusive with the previous one |
| `dryRun` | boolean | Preview the prompt without dispatching, see §6.4 |

**Advanced fields**

| Field | Validation | Notes |
|-------|------------|-------|
| `model` | ≤200 chars | Model ID for this new session |
| `reasoningEffort` | `low` / `medium` / `high` / `xhigh` / `max` / `ultra` | Reasoning effort for this new session |
| `steer` | boolean | Allow a follow-up to be merged into the running turn (Codex App only), see §6.5. Mutually exclusive with `dryRun` |
| `allowChatMessages` | boolean | Let this turn post messages to the group, see §6.6 |
| `suppressFinalOutput` | boolean | Only effective for **fire-and-forget + real group**: skip the closing reply in the group |

All boolean fields must be real booleans: `"true"` or `1` is a 400.

About `model` / `reasoningEffort`:

* Only these CLIs honor them: Codex, Codex App, TraeX, Remote Runner, Grok, Claude Code, Kimi, ZCode. Other CLIs ignore both fields.
* **Only for newly created sessions**: a turn appended to an existing session doesn't change the model.
* `reasoningEffort` is checked against the CLI/model; a level that's clearly unsupported returns 400.
* `model` only applies to this run and isn't saved on the session; after a daemon restart the bot's configured model is used. `reasoningEffort` is saved with the session.

**Two fields that look useful but nothing reads**

| Field | What actually happens |
|-------|------------------------|
| `dedupKey` | The trigger flow doesn't read it. It's only written into the model prompt and included in the idempotency payload comparison. Real event dedup lives in the [Webhook connector](/botmux/en/webhook.md)'s "dedup field" |
| `status` | Same (`firing` / `resolved` or any string). Note: changing `status` under the same `idempotencyKey` also yields **409** |

***

## 5. Where the task lands, and what Feishu shows

### 5.1 No target → virtual session (zero Feishu noise)

With none of the three target fields, the daemon creates a synthetic session:

| Mode | Session ID prefix |
|------|-------------------|
| Sync | `http_wait_` |
| Async | `http_async_` |
| `source.type: "headless"` | `headless_` |

These sessions **post no topic seed, no streaming card, no messages at all, and skip the group-membership check**. `target.chatId` in the response is this synthetic ID.

### 5.2 `chatId` → real group session

A real group ID is **never** a virtual session, even in sync/async mode:

* The daemon first checks the bot is in the group; if not → **403 `bot_not_in_chat`**.
* **Topic groups** (or regular groups in `new-topic` mode) get a new thread: the seed message is posted first and the session anchors on it.
* **Regular groups** follow the group's reply mode: an existing shared session is continued, `new-topic` opens a thread. A non-empty explicit `topicMessage` opens a dedicated thread in every mode except `shared`.

### 5.3 `chatId` + `rootMessageId` → append to an existing thread

No seed is posted. Rejected when:

* No `sessionId` and no `chatId` → 400 `target_required`.
* The message isn't visible or its group can't be resolved → 400 `target_required`.
* The message **doesn't belong** to the group you passed → `chat_not_allowed` (⚠️ currently **500** on this endpoint, see §11.3).

### 5.4 `sessionId` → add a turn to an existing session

The group is inherited from the session; no need to pass it.

* Session doesn't exist → **404 `session_not_found`**.
* Session can't take input yet (still picking a directory, first start, building a worktree, or waiting in the backlog) → `session_not_runnable` (currently HTTP 500). The input did **not** reach the CLI; retry later.
* With `turnIdempotencyKey` while the session is still in its opening activation → `trigger_failed` (message contains `session activation in progress`); retry later with the same key.

### 5.5 What the group actually sees

| Target × mode | Topic seed | Streaming card | Answer posted to Feishu | Answer returned to program |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| virtual + sync/async | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ |
| real group + fire-and-forget | ✓ (topic groups) | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ |
| **real group + sync/async** | ✓ (topic groups) | ✓ | **✗** | ✓ |
| existing thread + fire-and-forget | ✗ | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ |
| **existing thread + sync/async** | ✗ | ✓ | **✗** | ✓ |

> ⚠️ **The two bold rows are the usual trap**: in a real group with sync/async, members see the bot working but **never get the final answer** — it went to the HTTP caller. To show the answer in the group: use fire-and-forget, have your program post `output.content` back yourself, or use `allowChatMessages` on an existing group session (§6.6).

### 5.6 Want a new group created every time? Use a Webhook connector

`chatId` here must be an existing group. "Create a new group per event" is a delivery mode unique to [Webhook connectors](/botmux/en/webhook.md) (it also adds authorized users to the group and supports dedup by event field).

### 5.7 Two differences from chatting in Feishu

* **No worktree**: even if the bot has "auto-create worktree" on, virtual and sync/async sessions **always run in the base directory**, so programmatic calls don't leave a worktree behind each time. Only "real group + fire-and-forget + the bot's own default directory" gets an auto worktree.
* **Simpler working-directory choice**: oncall-bound directory → bot default directory (including `defaultOncall.workingDir`) → bot `workingDir` → `~`. Directories aren't inherited from sibling sessions (`botToBotSameDir` doesn't apply here), and oncall isn't auto-bound. If you need a fixed directory, configure it on the bot or oncall.

***

## 6. Execution modes in detail

### 6.1 Sync (`waitForFinalOutput`)

```bash
curl -X POST "http://<host>:7891/api/trigger" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -H "Cookie: botmux_dashboard_token=$TOKEN" \
  -d '{
    "source":{"type":"webhook"},
    "target":{"kind":"turn","botId":"cli_xxx"},
    "instruction":"Reply with exactly one line: SYNC_DEMO_OK",
    "envelope":{"format":"json","sourceName":"demo","trusted":false},
    "options":{"waitForFinalOutput":true,"timeoutMs":60000}
  }'
```

One request, one response; the result is right in `output.content`:

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "triggerId": "trg_dcbd124a-...",
  "action": "completed",
  "target": { "kind": "turn", "sessionId": "0bc442ef-...", "chatId": "http_wait_..." },
  "output": { "content": "SYNC_DEMO_OK" },
  "message": "queued new session turn and completed"
}
```

> Past `timeoutMs` you get **HTTP 504** + `wait_timeout`. The task **keeps running in the background**, but the timeout response has no `sessionId`, so you can never look it up. If you need a fallback query, use async.

### 6.2 Async (`asyncReturnSessionId`)

See §1 for the request. **Async is recommended for production**: you get a `sessionId` right away, can poll and stop, and results survive daemon restarts (§9, §10).

### 6.3 Fire-and-forget (neither flag)

Requires one of `chatId` / `sessionId` / `rootMessageId`. Returns immediately (`action` is `queued` or `delivered`); the answer goes out as a **normal Feishu reply**.

> ⚠️ This mode **doesn't record a result**. `trigger-result` only ever shows `running`, then `failed` once the session closes — **you never get `output.content`**. Use async or sync if your program needs the result.

### 6.4 `dryRun`: preview the prompt, don't dispatch

With `dryRun: true` no session is created and nothing is dispatched; you get back the prompt the model would receive:

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "triggerId": "trg_...",
  "action": "dry_run",
  "target": { "kind": "turn", "sessionId": null, "chatId": "oc_xxx" },
  "message": "would create or deliver a new session turn",
  "promptPreview": "<botmux_task trusted=\"true\">…"
}
```

* `promptPreview` is truncated past 4000 chars, with `...[truncated]` appended.
* `message` tells you where it would land: `would inject into existing session` for an existing session, otherwise `would create or deliver a new session turn`.

### 6.5 `steer`: merge a follow-up into the running turn (Codex App only)

`steer: true` allows a new message to be **merged into the Codex App turn that's currently running**, instead of queueing behind it. Handy for "also handle X" or "stop doing that, do Y instead" mid-task.

It's a **best-effort** permission, not a guarantee:

* **Send it on the first turn too**: Codex requires both the opening turn and later follow-ups to be explicitly authorized, so pass `steer: true` on the very first request.
* **Falls back automatically**: if there's no running turn, the turn is closing, it's a review/compaction turn, or the worker is cold-starting, the message becomes an ordinary queued follow-up. The request never fails because of `steer`.
* **Other CLIs**: the flag does nothing; messages queue as usual.

The response echoes `steer: true` only when the request was actually dispatched (not on idempotent reuse). The echo only means the daemon carried the permission — **not that the merge succeeded**.

**How results are attributed after a merge**: Codex produces **one merged answer** for the group. Every earlier request ends up with **the same merged text**:

* Async: earlier members poll to `completed` with the merged `output.content`, **without `usage`** (usage is recorded only on the newest trigger). A daemon restart during the merge is handled correctly.
* Sync: earlier members return together when the answer lands. Sync results live only in memory, though — if the daemon restarts mid-group, they just wait until their own timeout.

### 6.6 `allowChatMessages`: let this turn post to the group

By default, sync/async tasks are told "don't call `botmux send`, don't post to Feishu". If you want a turn to post to the group on its own (for example, to notify people), pass `allowChatMessages: true`:

* Applies to this turn only; it doesn't carry over to later turns.
* The final answer **still** goes back to the HTTP caller.
* Requirements: async mode + `target.sessionId` pointing to an **existing real group session** (not a DM, not a virtual session); can't be combined with sync, `steer`, or `source.type: "headless"`. Otherwise → 400 `bad_request`.

***

## 7. When there's nothing to say (`BOTMUX_NOTHING_TO_SEND`)

In sync/async mode (first turn and follow-ups alike), the daemon tells the model:

* Your reply is **returned verbatim to a program**, not shown in a chat.
* **Output only the final answer** — no preamble, no talk about these system notes.
* Don't call `botmux send` or post to Feishu (unless `allowChatMessages` is on).
* **If there's nothing to answer, output only `BOTMUX_NOTHING_TO_SEND`**; the program gets an empty result.

This token directly affects how the turn settles:

| Mode | When the model outputs only this token |
|------|-----------------------------------------|
| **Async** | Settles as `completed` with an **empty** `output.content` |
| **Sync** | There's no settle path for it; it waits until `timeoutMs`, then **504 `wait_timeout`** |

> ⚠️ This is the only semantic difference between sync and async. If a task **may not need an answer** (health checks, "report only if something's wrong"), use **async** — otherwise every "nothing happened" costs a full timeout.

If the model writes an answer and also ends with the token, the answer is returned and the token stripped. Only "nothing but the token" counts as an empty result.

***

## 8. Preventing duplicate runs (idempotency keys)

### 8.1 `idempotencyKey`: new sessions

**Problem**: after an async trigger, if the HTTP response is lost on the network (while the task is in fact running), your retry creates **a second session and runs the task again**.

**Fix**: generate a stable key and store it **before** sending the request; retry with the same key. The daemon returns **the same session and `triggerId` without dispatching again**:

```bash
curl -X POST "http://<host>:7891/api/trigger" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -H "Cookie: botmux_dashboard_token=$TOKEN" \
  -d '{
    "source":{"type":"webhook"},
    "target":{"kind":"turn","botId":"cli_xxx"},
    "instruction":"...",
    "envelope":{"format":"json","sourceName":"demo","trusted":false},
    "options":{"asyncReturnSessionId":true, "idempotencyKey":"my-task-42"}
  }'
```

* Hit on an existing key: response has `idempotent: true`; first creation: `idempotent: false`. Then poll with `sessionId` as usual.
* **Only for brand-new async virtual sessions**: `asyncReturnSessionId: true`, with no `sessionId` / `rootMessageId` / `chatId` and no `waitForFinalOutput` / `dryRun`. Any other combination with this key → 400.
* **Same key, different content → 409 `idempotency_conflict`**. The comparison covers `instruction`, `envelope`, `source`, `presentation` and the entire `options` (except the key itself), so changing `model`, `status` or `timeoutMs` also gives 409. Always retry with **the same key and the same content**.
* **On a daemon crash it prefers not running over running twice**: if the daemon crashes between "started dispatching" and "confirmed the result", it won't blindly rerun after restart; the key settles as `failed` (`no_output`, with `error` saying the previous dispatch outcome is unknown). Treat it as failed.
* The key → session mapping is kept permanently, so a late retry after completion still gets the same session.

### 8.2 `turnIdempotencyKey`: follow-up turns on an existing session

Use this key when appending a turn to an existing session (with `target.sessionId`). A retry with the same key lands on **the same turn (same `triggerId`) instead of injecting twice**, and the response has `idempotent: true`.

```bash
curl -X POST "http://<host>:7891/api/trigger" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -H "Cookie: botmux_dashboard_token=$TOKEN" \
  -d '{
    "source":{"type":"webhook"},
    "target":{"kind":"turn","botId":"cli_xxx","sessionId":"<existing session>"},
    "instruction":"...",
    "envelope":{"format":"json","sourceName":"demo","trusted":false},
    "options":{"asyncReturnSessionId":true, "turnIdempotencyKey":"my-followup-7"}
  }'
```

* Requirements: `target.sessionId` set, no `waitForFinalOutput` / `dryRun`. Works for both async and fire-and-forget: async results are polled as usual, fire-and-forget answers still go to Feishu.
* **Mutually exclusive** with `idempotencyKey`; both → 400. The two key spaces are separate — the same string never collides.
* Same key, different content → 409; crash behavior and retention match §8.1.

***

## 9. Polling for results

```
GET /api/sessions/:sessionId/trigger-result
    optional ?triggerId=<trg_...>: a specific trigger; otherwise the session's latest
```

**Normal responses are all HTTP 200 + `ok: true`; read the task state from `state` only**, not from `ok` or the HTTP status.

| `state` | Meaning | What to do |
|---------|---------|------------|
| `running` | Still running | Check again in a few seconds |
| `completed` | Result is ready | Read `output.content` (may be empty, see §7) |
| `interrupted` | You stopped this turn (§10.2); the session is still there | Treat as cancelled |
| `failed` | Session ended without a result | Soft terminal, see 9.2 |
| `not_found` | No such session | See 9.3 |

`completed` example:

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "state": "completed",
  "triggerId": "trg_87e7b415-...",
  "action": "completed",
  "output": { "content": "ASYNC_DEMO_OK" },
  "usage": { "inputTokens": 60, "outputTokens": 30, "cacheReadTokens": 40, "cacheCreateTokens": 0 },
  "finishedAt": "2026-07-24T08:43:17.126Z",
  "target": { "kind": "turn", "sessionId": "2eed60c4-...", "chatId": "http_async_..." },
  "async": { "status": "completed", "sessionId": "2eed60c4-...", "completedAt": "..." }
}
```

About `usage` (this turn's token usage):

* **Codex App tasks only**, and only when it was captured; otherwise the whole field is omitted. **No `usage` means "unknown", not 0.**
* The four numbers don't overlap: `inputTokens` (new input excluding cache), `outputTokens`, `cacheReadTokens`, `cacheCreateTokens`, all for this turn only.
* After a daemon restart, `usage` and `output` are restored from disk together.

### 9.1 Which triggers can reach `completed`

| Trigger | Can reach `completed` |
|---------|:---------------------:|
| Async (any target) | ✓ |
| Sync | ✗ (the result is in the trigger response) |
| Fire-and-forget | ✗ (stays `running`, then `failed` once the session closes) |

### 9.2 Don't give up on `failed` too quickly

| Situation | Returns |
|-----------|---------|
| Session ended without a result — **a real failure, or you closed the session yourself** | `errorCode: "no_output"` |
| Idempotency key hit a daemon crash; not rerun (at-most-once) | `no_output`, `error` says the previous dispatch outcome is unknown |
| The CLI explicitly reported this turn as failed | `errorCode: "trigger_failed"`, with the reason in `terminalErrorCode` |

Tips:

* Decide whether *you* cancelled it from your own records, not from `failed`.
* Treat `no_output` as "needs a second look": confirm there's really no result and you didn't cancel it, then mark it as finally failed.

### 9.3 `not_found` comes in two shapes

When querying through the Dashboard, treat both as "not found":

1. `HTTP 404` + `{ "ok": false, "error": "unknown_session" }`: the Dashboard has never seen this ID (usually a wrong or stale ID).
2. `HTTP 200` + `{ "ok": true, "state": "not_found" }`: the request reached the daemon, but there's nothing on disk either.

### 9.4 `?triggerId=` doesn't match

The session exists but never had the `triggerId` you gave → HTTP 400 + `ok: false` + `errorCode: "bad_request"`, **with no `state` field**. That's a malformed request, not "not found".

### 9.5 Webhook connector polling has a different shape

The [Webhook connector](/botmux/en/webhook.md)'s own polling endpoint rewrites `failed` and `not_found` into `ok: false` + **HTTP 404** (keeping `state`). This page's `/api/sessions/:id/trigger-result` doesn't. If you integrate with both, handle them separately.

***

## 10. Do results survive restarts? How do I stop a task?

### 10.1 Results survive restarts

**After a daemon restart, a finished async task still reads as `completed` (with `output.content`), never `not_found`.** The result is written to disk when it completes (`data/async-triggers/<sessionId>.json`).

So **don't conclude the task is lost** after one miss. Only start compensation once it's confirmed missing (`unknown_session` / `not_found`) and your own timeout has also expired.

### 10.2 Stop just this turn (keep the session)

```bash
curl -X POST "http://<host>:7891/api/sessions/:sessionId/turns/:triggerId/interrupt" \
  -H "Cookie: botmux_dashboard_token=$TOKEN"
# → { "ok": true, "action": "interrupted", "sessionId": "...", "triggerId": "..." }
```

Interrupts only the turn behind this one **async** trigger; the session stays and you can keep asking follow-ups. The daemon first confirms the CLI is running exactly this turn before sending the interrupt, so it never stops a different turn by mistake.

| Response | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| 200 `action: "interrupted"` | Stopped; `trigger-result` now shows `state: "interrupted"`. Repeated calls return `idempotent: true` |
| 404 `session_not_found` | Session doesn't exist or is closed |
| 404 `bad_request` | No async trigger with this `triggerId` in the session |
| 409 `trigger_failed` | The turn already ended, isn't running in this daemon generation, or the session is being transferred |
| 503 `trigger_failed` | The interrupt wasn't delivered or couldn't be saved; retry later or keep polling |

### 10.3 Close the whole session

```bash
curl -X POST "http://<host>:7891/api/sessions/:sessionId/close" \
  -H "Cookie: botmux_dashboard_token=$TOKEN"
# → { "ok": true, ... }
```

`close` **shuts down the whole session**. That's fine for a one-shot virtual session (one turn only); for a **real group session**, other people may be using it, so be careful — use §10.2 if you only want to stop one turn.

If there was no result before closing, polling afterwards returns `state: "failed"` (`no_output`). That's expected; handle it from your own cancellation records.

***

## 11. Response fields and status codes

### 11.1 Response fields

| Field | When present |
|-------|--------------|
| `ok` | Always |
| `triggerId` | Almost always (`trg_<uuid>`) |
| `action` | `queued` / `delivered` / `completed` / `dry_run`, see 11.2; the stop endpoint (§10.2) returns `interrupted` |
| `state` | Polling responses; on trigger responses only when an idempotency key hits an already finished task |
| `target` | `{ kind, sessionId?, chatId? }` |
| `output.content` | Sync completion, or polling reaches `completed` |
| `usage` | See §9 |
| `async` | `{ status: 'pending' \| 'completed', sessionId, completedAt? }` |
| `finishedAt` | End time (ISO 8601) |
| `message` | Human-readable explanation |
| `errorCode` / `error` | On errors, see 11.3 |
| `terminalErrorCode` | The specific reason when the CLI explicitly reported failure |
| `promptPreview` | `dryRun` only |
| `idempotent` | With an idempotency key: `true` = reused an existing session/turn |
| `idempotencyKey` / `turnIdempotencyKey` | Echo of your key |
| `steer` | See §6.5 |
| `readOnlyUrl` / `viewToken` | Only in core-only deployments (`BOTMUX_CORE_ONLY=1`) while the CLI terminal is alive: a read-only terminal link on polling responses, see [Core-only embedding](/botmux/en/api-core-only.md) |

### 11.2 `action` vs `message`

`action` only describes **dispatch** ("accepted"), not whether the task succeeded. There are only two ways to get the result: sync `output.content`, or async polling to `completed`.

| `action` | `message` | When |
|----------|-----------|------|
| `delivered` | `delivered to existing session` | Fire-and-forget; the existing session's CLI is running |
| `queued` | `durably queued behind the existing activation` | Same, but the session is still opening; this turn queues first |
| `queued` | `queued existing session turn` | Fire-and-forget; the existing session's CLI must be restarted |
| `queued` | `delivered to existing session; poll by sessionId or triggerId for final output` | Async + existing session |
| `queued` | `queued new session turn` | Fire-and-forget, new session |
| `queued` | `queued new session turn (building worktree)` | Same, worktree being built |
| `queued` | `queued new session turn; poll by sessionId or triggerId for final output` | Async + new session |
| `completed` | `delivered to existing session and completed` | Sync + existing session |
| `completed` | `queued new session turn and completed` | Sync + new session |
| `dry_run` | `would inject into existing session` / `would create or deliver a new session turn` | `dryRun` |

### 11.3 HTTP status codes

**Dashboard layer**

| Status | `errorCode` | Cause |
|:------:|-------------|-------|
| 400 | `bad_json` | Malformed JSON, or the body exceeds 512 KiB |
| 400 | `target_required` | Missing `target.botId` |
| 400 | others | Field validation failed (see §4) |
| 403 | `control_origin_forbidden` | Cross-site write request from a browser rejected (see note below) |
| 502 | `daemon_offline` | Forwarding to the daemon failed |
| 503 | `daemon_offline` | Target daemon isn't online |

> **About 403 `control_origin_forbidden`**: only non-read requests initiated by a browser that carry `Origin` or `Sec-Fetch-Site` and are judged cross-site (including a different port on the same host, sibling subdomains, and `Origin: null`) get it; it is a by-design rejection and retrying won't help. This gate applies both to this endpoint and to the session write endpoints under `/api/sessions/`. Non-browser callers such as curl, scripts, and CI that send neither of these source headers are unaffected and can call the API as before.

**Daemon layer**

| Status | `errorCode` | Cause |
|:------:|-------------|-------|
| 200 | — | Success (`queued` / `delivered` / `completed` / `dry_run`) |
| 200 | `no_output` etc. | `ok: false` but `state: "failed"`: an idempotency key hit an already failed task. The HTTP call itself succeeded; read `state` |
| 400 | `bad_json` / `bad_request` / `target_required` | Malformed request or invalid combination |
| 400 | `bot_not_found` | `botId` doesn't match this daemon |
| 403 | `bot_not_in_chat` | Bot isn't in the target group |
| 404 | `session_not_found` | `target.sessionId` doesn't exist |
| 409 | `idempotency_conflict` | Same key, different content |
| 410 | `legacy_workflow_retired` | `target.kind: "workflow"` (retired) |
| 503 | `bot_not_found` / `trigger_failed` | Daemon isn't ready yet |
| 504 | `wait_timeout` | Sync wait timed out |
| 500 | `trigger_failed` / `session_not_runnable` / `chat_not_allowed` etc. | Other failures |

⚠️ **On a 500, read `errorCode` before retrying**:

* `chat_not_allowed` (`rootMessageId` doesn't belong to the group you passed) is a **request error; retrying won't help**. Webhook connectors return 403 for the same code; this endpoint currently returns 500.
* `session_not_runnable` means the input wasn't delivered, so retrying later is safe.

### 11.4 Error codes

**You may see these on this endpoint**: `bad_json`, `bad_request`, `bot_not_found`, `bot_not_in_chat`, `chat_not_allowed`, `daemon_offline`, `idempotency_conflict`, `legacy_workflow_retired`, `no_output`, `session_not_found`, `session_not_runnable`, `target_required`, `trigger_failed`, `wait_timeout`

**Only on [Webhook connectors](/botmux/en/webhook.md)**

| Code | Status | Meaning |
|------|:------:|---------|
| `invalid_signature` | 401 | Token or signature check failed |
| `replay` | 401 | Signature timestamp outside the allowed window |
| `rate_limited` | 429 | Rate limit exceeded |
| `group_create_failed` | 501 / 502 | Group creation failed in "new group per event" mode |
| `lifecycle_extract_failed` | 400 | A dedup field is configured but missing from the event |

`dry_run` and `workflow_trigger_not_implemented` are also in the error-code list but are never returned.

***

## 12. Limits and caveats

* **Request body max 512 KiB** (checked at the Dashboard).
* **The Dashboard → daemon hop has no timeout**. A sync call with `timeoutMs: 300000` really holds for 5 minutes. **Set your own timeout on your HTTP client.**
* **API-only bots** (`apiOnly`, no Feishu transport) have four rules; breaking any is 400 `bad_request`:
  1. Sync or async is required;
  2. No `rootMessageId`;
  3. No real `chatId`;
  4. `sessionId` may only point to its own virtual session.
* **Async result files aren't cleaned up automatically yet**: files under `data/async-triggers/` only accumulate, so results stay queryable after a session closes.
* **`output.content` may occasionally start with a preamble line**. botmux tells the model to output only the answer and most results are clean, but it's not a hard guarantee. When showing it to users:
  * ✅ Strip only known fixed prefixes (e.g. `here's my answer:`) and keep everything after.
  * ❌ Don't "keep only the last paragraph": answers can legitimately be multi-paragraph or include code blocks.
  * Store the raw `content` for archives and audits.

***

## 13. Client example

```ts
// Minimal skeleton: async trigger + poll until done
async function runAndAwait(instruction: string, botId: string): Promise<Result> {
  // 1) Trigger async, get sessionId
  const trg = await post('/api/trigger', {
    source: { type: 'webhook' },
    target: { kind: 'turn', botId },
    instruction,
    envelope: { format: 'json', sourceName: 'my-system', trusted: false },
    options: { asyncReturnSessionId: true },
  });
  const sessionId = trg.target.sessionId;

  // 2) Poll, looking only at state
  for (;;) {
    const r = await getTriggerResult(sessionId);
    switch (r.state) {
      case 'running':
      case 'unknown':     await sleep(3000); continue;       // unknown: network/5xx, task may still be running
      case 'completed':   return { ok: true, content: r.output?.content ?? '' }; // empty string is a valid result
      case 'interrupted': return { ok: false, cancelled: true };
      case 'failed':      return { ok: false, needsReconcile: true }; // soft terminal; double-check
      case 'not_found':   return { ok: false, notFound: true };
      case 'error':       return { ok: false, fatal: true, why: r.why }; // request/auth error; retrying won't help
    }
  }
}

// Key point: separate "can't tell yet, retry" from "definitely over"
async function getTriggerResult(sessionId: string) {
  let res: Response;
  try {
    res = await fetch(`/api/sessions/${sessionId}/trigger-result`, { headers: cookie() });
  } catch (e) {
    return { state: 'unknown', why: `network: ${String(e)}` }; // network error → retry
  }

  if (res.status === 401 || res.status === 403) return { state: 'error', why: `auth ${res.status}` };

  if (res.status === 404) {
    const b = await res.json().catch(() => ({}));
    if (b?.error === 'unknown_session') return { state: 'not_found' };
    if (b?.state) return b; // Webhook connector polling rewrites failed/not_found to 404 (§9.5)
    // Any other 404 (e.g. HTML from a gateway) does NOT mean not found — retry it,
    // otherwise a gateway hiccup looks like a lost task and you dispatch it twice.
    return { state: 'unknown', why: 'opaque 404' };
  }

  if (res.status === 400) return { state: 'error', why: 'bad_request' }; // e.g. triggerId mismatch (§9.4)
  if (res.status >= 500) return { state: 'unknown', why: `upstream ${res.status}` };

  let body: any;
  try { body = await res.json(); } catch { return { state: 'unknown', why: 'non-json 2xx' }; }
  return body?.state ? body : { state: 'unknown', why: 'no state field' };
}
```

Key points:

* Clamp `timeoutMs` to `1000`–`300000`, and **set your own HTTP client timeout** (§12).
* On a sync 504 the task may still be running, but you have no `sessionId` to look it up. Use async if that matters.
* `output.content` on `completed` may be an empty string (§7) — that's a normal result.
* Keep **retryable** (network errors, 5xx, non-JSON) and **definitely over** (`not_found`, 400, 401/403) strictly apart, or you may dispatch twice.
* On a 500 from this endpoint, read `errorCode` first (§11.3).

***

## Appendix: endpoint cheat sheet

| Endpoint | Method | Purpose |
|----------|--------|---------|
| `/api/trigger` | POST | Trigger a task |
| `/api/sessions/:id/trigger-result` | GET | Poll async results (optional `?triggerId=`) |
| `/api/sessions/:id/turns/:triggerId/interrupt` | POST | Stop one async trigger; keep the session |
| `/api/sessions/:id` | GET | Session info (status, title, …) |
| `/api/sessions/:id/close` | POST | Close the whole session |

Related pages: [Webhook connectors](/botmux/en/webhook.md) (auto-created groups, signatures, dedup), [Core-only embedding](/botmux/en/api-core-only.md) (API-only deployment without Feishu).

# Architecture overview

<video src="../img/video-v9-architecture-en.mp4" controls preload="metadata" style="width:100%;border-radius:8px"></video>

What botmux does fits in one sentence: **it turns Lark messages into input for an AI coding CLI, and turns the CLI's output back into Lark cards.** This page covers which processes make up botmux, how a message flows through them, and what happens on restart. You don't need any of this for day-to-day use; come back when you're troubleshooting or contributing.

## The big picture

![botmux processes: the supervisor starts a daemon per bot, the Dashboard and plugin services; each daemon runs a worker per topic, which reaches the CLI through a session backend such as tmux](/img/arch-overview-en.png)

## What each process does

| Process | How many | What it does |
|---------|----------|--------------|
| supervisor | 1 per machine | This is what `botmux start` launches. It starts each bot's daemon, the Dashboard and plugin services, and restarts any of them that crash |
| daemon | **1 per bot** | Holds the Lark long connection, decides whether a message should be handled and which session it belongs to, handles slash commands, and creates, restores and closes sessions |
| worker | 1 per active topic | Launches the CLI through an adapter, types Lark messages into it, and turns terminal output into streaming cards; also serves the session's [web terminal](/botmux/en/web-terminal.md) |
| CLI process | 1 per topic | The AI coding CLI doing the actual work, running inside tmux or another backend, exactly as if you used it in your own terminal |
| dashboard | 1 per machine | The [admin dashboard](/botmux/en/dashboard.md), port 7891 by default |

Key points:

* **One daemon per bot, fully isolated.** A problem in one bot won't take the others down. See [Multi-bot](/botmux/en/multi-bot.md).
* **A "session backend" sits between the worker and the CLI.** The default is tmux: the CLI lives inside tmux, so restarting the worker or daemon doesn't interrupt it.
* Want to drive a CLI over HTTP without Lark at all? Use the single-process [Core-only mode](/botmux/en/api-core-only.md). It skips the supervisor and doesn't need `bots.json`.

## How a message flows

![How a message flows: Lark push, daemon filtering, command classification, find or create the session, output to cards](/img/arch-message-flow-en.png)

Take "@ the bot in a topic and say something" as an example:

1. **Lark pushes the message to the daemon.** The daemon first decides whether to handle it: was the bot @-mentioned, is this a topic it owns, does the sender have permission.
2. **Slash commands are recognized.** Messages starting with `/` are classified against the command table (e.g. `/close`, `/restart`) and either handled by the daemon or passed to the CLI. Full list in [Slash commands](/botmux/en/slash-commands.md).
3. **The session is found or created.** A new topic starts a new worker and CLI; an existing session is reused and the message is typed into the running CLI.
4. **Output becomes cards.** The worker keeps reading the CLI's output, converts it to Markdown, updates the streaming card in Lark in real time, and posts the final reply when the turn ends.
5. **The CLI can also send messages on its own.** botmux injects a set of built-in Skills into the CLI (such as `botmux-send`, `botmux-schedule`, `botmux-history`), which it uses to post to the topic, create scheduled tasks, read chat history and more. See [Skills and CLI commands](/botmux/en/skill-cli.md).

## What happens on restart

![What survives a restart per session backend: tmux and other persistent backends keep the CLI, pty restarts it](/img/arch-restart-en.png)

`botmux restart` restarts the daemon and workers. Whether the CLI restarts too depends on the session backend:

| Backend | How to enable | After a daemon restart |
|---------|---------------|------------------------|
| **tmux** (default) | Nothing to configure | The CLI keeps running; the next message reattaches automatically and context is kept |
| zmx / zellij / herdr | Set explicitly via `backendType` or `BACKEND_TYPE` | Also persistent; requires the matching tool |
| pty | Set explicitly via `BACKEND_TYPE=pty` or `backendType: "pty"` | The CLI exits with the worker and is relaunched after restart |

If tmux isn't available, botmux **does not silently fall back to pty**. It blocks new sessions and shows a card asking you to install tmux. Details in [Persistent tmux sessions](/botmux/en/tmux.md) and [ZMX backend](/botmux/en/zmx.md).

On startup the daemon automatically restores previously active sessions, so you can keep chatting in your Lark topics after a restart.

## Where files live

| Path | Contents |
|------|----------|
| `~/.botmux/bots.json` | Bot configuration, see [bots.json](/botmux/en/bots-json.md) |
| `~/.botmux/.env` | Global environment variables, see [Environment variables](/botmux/en/env.md) |
| `~/.botmux/data/` | Session data, one SQLite database per bot (`session-stores/<appId>/sessions.db`) |
| `~/.botmux/logs/` | Logs: `daemon-<index>-out.log` / `-err.log`, `dashboard-out.log` and so on; or just run `botmux logs` |

## Source map (for contributors)

If you want to change the code, start here:

| Location | Responsibility |
|----------|----------------|
| `src/cli.ts`, `src/cli/` | The `botmux` command-line entry and its subcommands |
| `src/index-supervisor.ts`, `src/core/fleet-supervisor.ts` | Supervisor: starts and watches daemons, the dashboard and plugin services |
| `src/daemon.ts` | Daemon orchestration layer that wires the modules together |
| `src/worker.ts` | Worker process: manages the CLI, renders cards, serves the web terminal |
| `src/bot-registry.ts`, `src/config.ts` | Loading `bots.json` and global config |
| `src/adapters/cli/` | CLI adapters, one file per CLI (launch args, input method, Skill directory, etc.) |
| `src/adapters/backend/` | Session backends: tmux, pty, zmx, zellij, herdr and more |
| `src/core/` | Session management, command table and routing (`command-schema.ts` / `command-router.ts`), worker pool, scheduler, etc. |
| `src/im/lark/` | Lark: event dispatch, card building and callbacks, API calls, message parsing |
| `src/skills/` | Built-in Skills injected into the CLI |
| `src/dashboard/` | Admin dashboard |
| `src/utils/` | Idle detection, terminal screenshot rendering, logging and other utilities |

For the full steps to add a new CLI, see `src/adapters/cli/CLAUDE.md` in the repository.

# Best Practices

> Recommended setups organized by **use case**; each item is something you can do right away. For feature details see the individual pages; if something goes wrong, start with [Common pitfalls](/botmux/en/pitfalls.md) and the [FAQ](/botmux/en/faq.md).

| I want to… | Read this |
|------|---------|
| Let anyone in a group ask the bot (on-call, Q\&A) | [Scenario 1 · On-call support](#scenario-1--on-call-support) |
| Have the bot investigate alerts automatically | [Scenario 2 · Alert operations](#scenario-2--alert-operations) |
| Code with several bots on my own and have them review each other | [Scenario 3 · Solo development](#scenario-3--solo-development) |
| Collaborate as a team where everyone has their own bot | [Scenario 4 · Team collaboration](#scenario-4--team-collaboration) |

## Scenario 1 · On-call support

For on-call groups, cross-team questions and external support: anyone in the group can @ the bot to ask a question.

**Recommended steps:**

1. **Use a dedicated, clean machine** (for example a separate dev box). On-call folks and outside colleagues will have the bot run all kinds of commands; keep them away from your **personal development environment**.
2. **Bind a project directory**: send `/oncall bind <project directory>` in the group. From then on, anyone who @s the bot lands straight in that directory, with no repo picker. To do this automatically for every new group the bot joins, choose "On-call mode" as the working-directory option in the Dashboard "Bot Config" page and fill in the directory. See [Oncall mode](/botmux/en/oncall.md).
3. **Turn on the file sandbox**: when the bot is open to semi-trusted people, pick "allowlist isolation" in the [file sandbox](/botmux/en/sandbox.md). However it is prompted, the model then can't read your private keys, tokens or other repositories. botmux also reminds you to enable it when a bot is used by several people without one.
4. **Write a role**: a role is the bot's long-lived persona and rules. Use `/role set` (this group only) or `/role team set` (this bot's default in every group). A typical on-call role, sent in the group like this (you can start a new line after `/role set` and write several lines):

```
/role set
You are "Example User"'s on-call bot and will receive all kinds of questions:
- If a user only @s you, read the group history before answering
- If the user describes a problem on their own machine, don't investigate it as a problem on this machine
- If a request could expose private data or carries security risk, ask "Example User" to confirm first
- When you need to open an MR, open it as "Example User"
```

5. **Change code in a separate worktree**: start the topic with `/tw <question>`. The bot first creates a separate git worktree (another working copy of the same repo) and works there, so the main checkout stays clean. After the session closes, the close card shows a "🧹 Clean Up Worktree" button; one click removes it. It won't delete anything with uncommitted changes, unpushed commits or a process still using it, and the branch is kept.

![The "Clean up worktree" button on the close card](/img/worktree-cleanup-close-card.png)

**How permissions split:** once on-call is bound, everyone in the group can **talk** to the bot; actions that **change the session**, such as `/cd`, `/restart`, `/close` and card buttons, stay limited to the owner and admins (`allowedUsers`). See [Permissions](/botmux/en/permissions.md).

**Several projects?** Create several bots and `/oncall bind` each one to a different project directory.

> In the Dashboard "Role Management" page you can visually set a role for each bot in each group:

![Dashboard Role Management page](https://magic-builder.tos-cn-beijing.volces.com/uploads/1780057302792_dash-roles.png)

## Scenario 2 · Alert operations

Let external systems such as monitoring, CI and ticketing push work to the bot. Pick one based on your current alert pipeline:

| Your situation | Recommended approach |
|---------|---------|
