url: /botmux/en/model-proxy.md
---

# Model Proxy (Experimental)

> ⚠️ Experimental: endpoints, fields and limits may change. It does not affect regular Feishu bots.

`botmux model-proxy serve` starts an **authenticated, OpenAI Chat Completions–compatible endpoint** on `127.0.0.1`. Tools that only speak the OpenAI protocol (scripts built on the OpenAI SDK, code-review tools, and so on) can point their `baseURL` here and call models through a CLI's **own login** (Codex, Claude Code, …) — no separate API key needed.

```text
Your tool (OpenAI SDK)
   │  HTTP + Bearer token, 127.0.0.1 only
   ▼
botmux model-proxy (this page)
   │  local signed IPC
   ▼
Dedicated core-only instance (apiOnly bot with its own native login)
   │
   ▼
Native CLI model call (all tools disabled, inference only)
```

## When to use it

| I want to… | Use this? |
|---|---|
| Let an existing OpenAI-protocol tool reuse a CLI's model login | ✅ That's what it's for |
| My tool manages context and tool calls itself and only needs a "model endpoint" | ✅ Tool calls come back as **proposals**; your tool executes them |
| Have AI work and edit code in Feishu | ❌ Use a regular bot, see [Quick Start](/botmux/en/quickstart.md) |
| Drive a full CLI session over HTTP (read/write files, run commands) | ❌ See [Core-only (apiOnly) API control](/botmux/en/api-core-only.md) |
| Streaming, embeddings, images, audio, direct browser access | ❌ Not supported yet |

Key points up front:

* **Loopback only** (`127.0.0.1`). The config only accepts this address, so it is not reachable from the network.
* **The CLI never touches your files**: native CLI tools are disabled on every call; it only does inference. Returned `tool_calls` are proposals — execution stays with your tool.
* **No borrowed logins**: the proxy only uses the login in the dedicated bot directory you specify. It never picks up chat bots', the global, or other bots' credentials.

## Quick start

### Step 1: Start a dedicated core-only instance

The proxy doesn't call models itself. It forwards requests to a **separate core-only instance** (a botmux that doesn't connect to Feishu and only serves local HTTP, see [Core-only](/botmux/en/api-core-only.md)). That instance must:

* Be its own process with its own data directory and port. **Do not reuse — or restart for this — a running Feishu bot daemon.**
* Have a bot ID of the form `local_<name>`, using only letters, digits, `_` and `-` in the name (the proxy config rejects `.`).
* Use one of the supported CLIs below, with a native login completed in that bot's dedicated directory.

```bash
export STATE_DIR="$HOME/model-proxy-demo"     # pick a fresh directory
export BOTMUX_CORE_CLI=codex                  # or claude-code / pi / opencode
export BOTMUX_API_ONLY_BOT=local_reasoner
export BOTMUX_CORE_CODEX_AUTH_SYNC=isolated   # Codex only
export BOTMUX_CORE_STATE_DIR="$STATE_DIR/data"
export BOTMUX_API_PORT=8930                   # pick a free port
botmux serve --api-only
```

This command runs in the foreground. Use another terminal for the next steps, and `export STATE_DIR=...` again there (same directory as above).

Login files live under `$STATE_DIR/bots/<bot ID>/<subdir>`:

| CLI | Subdir | Login files needed |
|---|---|---|
| `codex` / `codex-app` | `codex` | `auth.json`, plus a `models_cache.json` that contains the target model; `BOTMUX_CORE_CODEX_AUTH_SYNC=isolated` is required |
| `claude-code` | `claude` | `.credentials.json` (a login that only lives in the system keychain won't work) |
| `pi` | `pi` | `auth.json` (API key or OAuth; executable helpers not supported) |
| `opencode` | `opencode` | `auth.json` (API / OAuth records only) |

For Codex, for example, log that directory in with `CODEX_HOME="$STATE_DIR/bots/local_reasoner/codex" codex login`.

> Keep this instance "plain": no sandbox, no `--backend`, no extra env vars, startup commands or wrapper. With any of these, the proxy refuses to start with `inference_profile_unsupported`.

### Step 2: Write the proxy config file

Save the following to a file, e.g. `$STATE_DIR/model-proxy.json`:

```json
{
  "port": 8788,
  "models": {
    "review-model": {
      "bot": "local_reasoner",
      "model": "<native-model-id>",
      "deadlineMs": 120000
    }
  },
  "clients": [
    { "id": "review-client", "tokenEnv": "BOTMUX_MODEL_PROXY_TOKEN", "models": ["review-model"] }
  ]
}
```

Lock it down so only you can read and write it, otherwise the proxy won't start:

```bash
export PROXY_CONFIG="$STATE_DIR/model-proxy.json"
chmod 600 "$PROXY_CONFIG"
```

* It must be a **regular file owned by the current user with mode exactly `0600`**.
* Its directory (and the directories above it) must not be writable by other users.

### Step 3: Create a token and start the proxy

```bash
# At least 32 characters, no whitespace; hand it to the tool over a secure channel
export BOTMUX_MODEL_PROXY_TOKEN="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
# Point at the data directory of the Step 1 instance so the proxy can find it
export SESSION_DATA_DIR="$STATE_DIR/data"
botmux model-proxy serve --config "$PROXY_CONFIG"
```

On success it prints one line of JSON:

```json
{"listening":"http://127.0.0.1:8788/v1","protocol":"chat-completions-v1"}
```

The proxy runs in the foreground. `Ctrl+C` (SIGINT) or SIGTERM stops it and cancels calls still in flight.

### Step 4: Connect your tool

```javascript
import OpenAI from 'openai';

const client = new OpenAI({
  baseURL: 'http://127.0.0.1:8788/v1',
  apiKey: process.env.BOTMUX_MODEL_PROXY_TOKEN,
  maxRetries: 0, // retries are your call; send an Idempotency-Key if you need dedup
});

const result = await client.chat.completions.create({
  model: 'review-model', // the alias from the config, not the native model name
  messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'Explain binary search in one sentence.' }],
});
console.log(result.choices[0].message.content);
```

To check connectivity first, list the models this token can use:

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8788/v1/models \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOTMUX_MODEL_PROXY_TOKEN"
```

## Config file reference

### Top-level fields

| Field | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `host` | No | Must be `127.0.0.1` (the default) |
| `port` | No | Listening port, default `8788`; `0` lets the OS pick one |
| `models` | Yes | Model **alias** table, at least one entry |
| `clients` | Yes | Clients allowed to connect, 1–100 |

Unknown fields in the config are rejected, not ignored.

### `models`: model aliases

Clients only see the alias (e.g. `review-model`), never which bot or native model is behind it.

| Field | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `bot` | Yes | Bot ID of the Step 1 dedicated instance, e.g. `local_reasoner` |
| `model` | Yes | Native model name, as understood by the CLI |
| `reasoningEffort` | No | Reasoning effort: `none` / `minimal` / `low` / `medium` / `high` / `xhigh` / `max` / `ultra`; ultimately bounded by what the CLI supports |
| `deadlineMs` | No | Per-call time limit, 100–300000 ms, default `120000`; returns 504 on timeout |

### `clients`: clients and tokens

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| `id` | Client name (letters, digits, `_`, `-`), must be unique |
| `tokenEnv` | **Name of the env var holding the token** (starts with an uppercase letter, e.g. `BOTMUX_MODEL_PROXY_TOKEN`). The token itself never goes in the config file |
| `models` | Aliases this client may use; all must exist in `models` |

* Tokens must be at least 32 characters with no whitespace; different clients can't share a token.
* The token is **unrelated** to the CLI's subscription credentials — it only decides which aliases are allowed.
* Changing a token requires restarting the proxy.

## Supported endpoints and fields

There are only two endpoints, both requiring `Authorization: Bearer <token>`:

* `GET /v1/models`: lists the aliases this token may use.
* `POST /v1/chat/completions`: **non-streaming** chat completion; `Content-Type` must be `application/json`.

| Field | Support |
|---|---|
| `model` | Required; an alias that is in this client's allow list |
| `messages` | Five roles: `system` / `developer` / `user` / `assistant` / `tool`; content is a string or an array of `text` parts only; up to 2000 messages |
| `tools` | `function` type only, up to 128; parameter schema must be an object |
| `tool_choice` | `auto` / `none` / `required` / a specific function |
| `parallel_tool_calls` | When `false`, at most one call proposal is returned |
| `response_format` | `text`, `json_object`, `json_schema` |
| `stream` / `n` | Omit them, or use `stream: false`, `n: 1` |
| `max_completion_tokens` | Omitted or `null` means no limit specified; an integer 1–128000 is **only supported by Claude Code** — other CLIs return 400 `max_completion_tokens_unsupported` |
| Anything else | Always 400 `unsupported_or_invalid_parameter`, including `temperature`, `top_p`, `max_tokens`, `seed`, `stop`, `logprobs`, etc. — **never silently ignored** |

Supported JSON Schema keywords for tool parameters and `json_schema`: `type`, `properties`, `required`, boolean `additionalProperties`, `items`, `enum`, `description`, `title`, numeric bounds, string length, array length. `$ref`, combinators like `anyOf`/`oneOf`, regex patterns and the like are not supported and are rejected.

### Multi-turn tool calls

Same as with OpenAI: the model returns `tool_calls` → your tool executes them → send the results back as `tool` messages (with `tool_call_id`) in the next request. The proxy checks that history is complete:

* `tool_call_id`s must be unique, and every call needs a matching result.
* No other message may be inserted before all results are in.

The model's answer is validated too: calling an unknown function, arguments that don't match the schema, violating `tool_choice`, or invalid JSON when JSON was requested all return 502 instead of handing you a bad result as success.

### What comes back

* On success `finish_reason` is `stop` or `tool_calls`. `length` is never returned.
* Tool call IDs are generated deterministically, so replaying an idempotent request keeps the same IDs.
* The standard `usage` field is always `null`. Real usage is in `botmux.native_invocation_usage`, which totals the **whole CLI invocation** (possibly including internal retries) and can't be treated as a single API bill. Some tools display `null` as 0 — that doesn't mean nothing was consumed.

## Idempotency and timeouts

* With an `Idempotency-Key` header (alphanumerics and `_.:-`, up to 128 chars), the same key + same request from the same client and alias replays the stored result without calling the CLI again; same key with a different request returns 409.
* Two requests without a key are two independent calls.
* A client disconnect cancels the call; within one proxy process, if several connections wait on the same result, one disconnecting doesn't affect the others.
* Run one proxy process per inference bot.

## Common errors

Errors always look like `{"error":{"message":"<code>","type":"...","param":...,"code":"<code>"}}` and never include CLI error output, credentials or local paths.

| Status | Common causes |
|---|---|
| 400 | Unsupported or malformed field (check which field `param` points to), incomplete tool history |
| 401 | Wrong token or missing `Authorization` |
| 403 | Alias not allowed for this token; or the request carries an `Origin` header (direct browser access isn't supported) |
| 404 | Unsupported endpoint |
| 409 | Idempotency key conflict, or the call was cancelled |
| 413 | Request body over 1 MB, or the assembled prompt is too long |
| 415 | `Content-Type` isn't `application/json`, or a content encoding was used |
| 429 | Inference instance is at capacity |
| 502 | Inference failed or the model output failed validation, e.g. `native_auth_missing` (dedicated directory not logged in), `native_model_not_found` (wrong model name) |
| 503 | Dedicated instance not found (`inference_profile_offline`), instance config doesn't qualify (`inference_profile_unsupported`), transport failure |
| 504 | `deadlineMs` exceeded |

## FAQ

**Startup fails with `model_proxy_config_missing` or a permission error?**
Check that the `--config` path exists, the file is `chmod 600`, and its directory isn't writable by other users.

**Startup fails with `model_proxy_token_requires_32_nonwhitespace_characters`?**
The env var named by `tokenEnv` isn't set, or the token is too short or contains whitespace.

**Getting `inference_profile_offline`?**
The proxy can't find the dedicated instance. Make sure it's running and that `SESSION_DATA_DIR` points at its data directory (`$STATE_DIR/data` from Step 1) when you start the proxy.

**Is it exactly the same as calling the model API directly?**
Not exactly. Conversation roles and tool definitions are serialized into text for the CLI, then the response is rebuilt from structured output. Role order and tool associations are preserved, but this isn't native verbatim passthrough, and the CLI's internal prompts and retries also affect results.

**Can the output limit be used as a cost cap?**
No. `max_completion_tokens` only applies to Claude's generation request; the CLI's wrapping and retries also consume tokens.

## Related

* [Core-only (apiOnly) API control](/botmux/en/api-core-only.md): starting the dedicated instance, data directory and security boundaries
* [CLI commands](/botmux/en/cli-commands.md)
* [Supported CLIs](/botmux/en/adapters.md)

import video_v4_multibot_en from '../../static/img/video-v4-multibot-en.mp4';

# Multi-bot Collaboration

You can run several Lark bots on one machine, each backed by a different CLI (say, one Claude Code and one Codex). Put them in the same group and different models can work together and pick holes in each other's work.

<video src={video_v4_multibot_en} controls preload="metadata" style={{width:'100%',borderRadius:'8px'}} />

## Get started in three steps

1. Each bot is one Lark app. Configure the CLI each one should use (see [bots.json](/botmux/en/bots-json.md)).
2. Add these bots and yourself to the same group (to create a group in one sentence, see [One-click session group](/botmux/en/group.md)).
3. @ the bot you want in the group and start talking.

Each bot is a separate process; they don't affect each other.

## Common scenarios

| What you want | How |
|---|---|
| Code review | Have Claude Code and Codex review the same MR and challenge each other where they disagree |
| Design review | Two AIs each propose a design, then look for flaws in the other's |
| Write/review split | One writes, one reviews, iterate until they converge |

## Who gets the message: routing rules

| Who is in the group | Do you need an @? |
|---|---|
| Just you + one bot | No. Just talk and it replies |
| Several humans, or several bots | Yes, @ the one you want (a single bot with several humans still needs an @) |

* `@botA @botB /t <task>`: **each** mentioned bot opens its own independent session on this message. Both bots share the same thread (anchored on your `/t` message), but the sessions are unrelated.
* To make one bot the "default responder" in a multi-bot group (replies without an @, but steps aside when someone else is named), set its mention policy to `ambient`. See [Mention policy](/botmux/en/mention-mode.md).

## Letting bots hand off to each other

Bots hand off by **actually @-mentioning** each other in a message.

> One rule to remember: **if you don't `--mention` the other bot, it is never triggered.**

How:

1. See who is in the group: run `botmux bots list` inside a session. It lists the bots in the current group, each with its `openId`, capability tag (`capability`), and `mentionable` (whether it can be reliably @-mentioned). The `<available_bots>` block in incoming messages also hints which bots can take a handoff.
2. Then @ the other bot: `botmux send --mention <other openId> "..."`. Once it receives the @, it starts working.

If `mentionable` is `false`, there is no reliable @ handle for that bot in this group yet. Send `/introduce` in the group so the bots register each other, and precise @-mentions work from then on.

### How bots find each other

* **Within one deployment**: by default, bots in the current group are discovered from the Lark group bot roster. Bots on the same machine can always talk to each other; bots on the same machine with the same owner can also run admin commands on each other, see [Permissions](/botmux/en/permissions.md#bots-on-this-machine-admin-commands-and-delegated-grants-trustsameownerbots).
* **Across deployments** (bots on someone else's machine): two paths, both going through the same team-trust gate with no `/grant` needed:
  * Federation in the Dashboard "Teams" panel: bring another deployment into the same team, then create cross-deployment groups;
  * Central-platform team sync: the platform pushes down teams and groups (see "Team scope" below).

A plain `/group` or the Dashboard "New group" flow creates an ordinary group inside your deployment. It uses neither path and carries no cross-deployment team trust.

## Letting bots that weren't @-mentioned catch up

By default a bot only sees messages that @ it. With **group context sharing** on, a bot automatically gets the group background it missed when it is woken up.

The owner or a human in `allowedUsers` @-mentions any bot managed by this deployment in the group and sends:

```text
@bot /context-sharing on       # enable
@bot /context-sharing status   # check status
@bot /context-sharing off      # disable
```

What happens once it's on:

* Bots in this deployment quietly "listen" to the group in the background, but **listening never starts a model**, so listening itself costs no tokens.
* When a bot is later woken up under the usual @ rules, it automatically receives the group messages it missed (with sources). The @ rules themselves don't change.
* One switch covers the whole group; no per-bot setup.

Limits and details:

| Item | Details |
|---|---|
| How much per turn | Up to 24,000 characters by default, counted toward that turn's model input tokens |
| Retention | 30 days, or at most 10,000 messages per group |
| What's included | Only published group messages and resource references; no DMs, hidden reasoning, unpublished tool results, or private files |
| Incomplete history | Gaps are clearly marked |
| Not supported | Cannot be enabled in DMs or API virtual sessions; sessions with `promptInjection=none` receive no automatic background |

`status` and the enable reply include a **recall sync** diagnostic, telling you whether recalled messages will be removed from the background in time:

| Result | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `subscribed` | The Lark app is verified to subscribe to the `im.message.recalled_v1` event (configuration only; doesn't guarantee every push arrives) |
| `update_submitted` | The subscription was submitted; you still need to publish a new app version in the Lark Developer Console |
| unknown / login session unavailable / stale | Historical background may temporarily keep recalled messages; check that event in the Developer Console, then rerun `status` |

Turning the switch off does no subscription check or setup.

## Team scope: finding bots on other people's machines

Once connected to the central platform, you can find bots **in your team on other people's machines** by **specialty** (even if they aren't in your group yet), then bring them into a group. Three commands, one job each:

```bash
# 1. Discover: list bots that have joined your team (use --team if this machine is in several teams)
botmux bots list --scope team [--team <teamId>]

# 2. New group: put the bots you found (by appId) and their owners into a new platform-created group
botmux create-group --team <teamId> --agent <appId> [--agent ...] [--name "Group name"]

# 3. Add to an existing group: add bots and their owners to a group you're already in
botmux bots invite --chat <chatId> --team <teamId> --agent <appId> [--agent ...]
```

If this machine belongs to only one team, `--team` can be omitted; with several teams it is required.

Each bot returned by `bots list --scope team` has:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `appId` | Use it to create groups and invite |
| `name` | Name |
| `specialties` | Specialty tags |
| `mentionable` / `online` | Whether it can be @-mentioned / is online |
| `owner` | Its owner |
| `machineId` / `machineName` | Which machine it runs on |

Key points:

* **Only bots that joined the team are listed**: the list only includes bots whose owner explicitly added them to the team in the platform's "Manage bots". If a bot is missing, its owner most likely hasn't added it yet.
* **Specialties and online status are self-reported**: `specialties` / `mentionable` / `online` are for picking only, not trusted credentials.
* **appId, not @**: you can't @ someone else's bot before it's in your group, so all three commands go by appId + platform auth. Permissions and team membership are decided entirely by the platform.
* **Target group for `bots invite`**: **you must already be in it**, and **the platform bot must be in it**. If the platform bot is missing, botmux automatically uses one of your local bots already in the group to add it, then retries; usually you won't notice. You're asked to add it manually only when the group requires owner approval to add bots, or none of your local bots is in that group.

### Three ways to add bots, don't mix them up

| Method | Use it for |
|---|---|
| `botmux create-group --team` | Put same-team bots from other machines, plus their owners, into a **new group** |
| `botmux bots invite` | Add same-team bots and their owners to a **group you're already in** |
| Lark in-group `/invite` | Add a same-tenant bot to the **current group** |

To create a group with only your local bots, use `botmux create-group --bot <name>` or [One-click session group](/botmux/en/group.md).

## Related

* [Roles & Teams](/botmux/en/roles.md): give each bot a persona and capability tags
* [One-click session group](/botmux/en/group.md): add several bots to a new group in one sentence
* [Session Relay](/botmux/en/relay.md): move a session into a collaboration group
* [Multi-topic collaboration](/botmux/en/multi-topic.md): let one bot open sub-topics and dispatch tasks to other bots
* [Project Progress Card](/botmux/en/project-card.md): the lead bot pins a card in the group that rolls up every sub-task's progress

url: /botmux/en/multi-topic.md
---

# Multi-Topic Orchestration Mode

<video src="../img/video-v4-multibot-en.mp4" controls preload="metadata" style="width:100%;border-radius:8px"></video>

Hand a big task to a main bot and it will:

* split the task into a few sub-projects;
* open a **child topic** in the group for each sub-project and send a group of bots in to work in parallel (a common pairing: one writes code, one reviews);
* use a **Lark task checklist** as the shared progress board;
* collect the results when every group is done and summarize them for you.

An ordinary group turns into a parallel workbench. It builds on [multi-bot collaboration](/botmux/en/multi-bot.md).

![Multi-topic orchestration · Lark task board as a shared progress board](https://magic-builder.tos-cn-beijing.volces.com/uploads/1780419243796_multitopic-board.png)

## When to use it

| What you need | Use |
|---|---|
| A long-running project where **several bots split the work**, each pushing forward in its own topic, while the main bot keeps tracking and does the final acceptance | Multi-topic orchestration (this page) |
| Just hand the next step or one focused job to another bot | @ it in the current topic to hand off (see [multi-bot collaboration](/botmux/en/multi-bot.md)); **no** new topic is opened |
| A bounded multi-step task that ends when it's done and produces one deliverable (e.g. "research, then write a report") | [Workflow](/botmux/en/workflow.md) |
| A pinned card in the group that shows the goal, to-dos, blockers, and every sub-task's status in one place | [Project Progress Card](/botmux/en/project-card.md) (works together with this page) |

## How to use

Just tell the main bot, for example:

> "Use multi-topic orchestration mode to split ×× into a few sub-projects and run them in parallel."
>
> "You be the orchestrator and coordinate a few bots to push this requirement forward in parallel."

The main bot then goes through these steps:

```
You state the requirement
  │
  ▼
① Main bot splits it into sub-projects and posts a "sub-project ↔ bot" plan ──► waits for you (edit it or assign bots yourself)
  │
  ▼
② Creates a Lark task checklist, one task per sub-project, and adds you as a member ──► you see it in Lark Tasks
  │
  ▼
③ Opens a child topic per sub-project and brings the assigned bots in
  │
  ▼
④ When a child bot finishes: marks its task done, then reports back to the main bot's topic
  │
  ▼
⑤ Main bot collects results, starts the next batch (if there are dependencies), and finally sends you a summary
```

You only do three things: **state the requirement → confirm the assignment → watch progress / collect results**. Opening topics, splitting work and reporting back all happen among the bots. Without your confirmation, the main bot neither creates the board nor dispatches any work.

## Before you start

* **Add the bots that should take part to this group** and make sure they can be @-mentioned (see [multi-bot collaboration](/botmux/en/multi-bot.md)). The main bot checks which collaborating bots are in the group before dispatching.
* Nothing else needs to be set up in advance: the main bot picks a working directory for each child bot when dispatching, so the child session starts right in that directory with no "pick a repo" card. If a child bot already has a default working directory, or has bound [OnCall](/botmux/en/oncall.md) in this group itself, the main bot can skip setting one and the child bot uses its own directory.

## While the work is running

| You want to | Do this |
|---|---|
| See overall progress | Open the task checklist in Lark Tasks, or look at the "task-tree card" below |
| See details of one sub-project | Open its child topic and watch the bot work as usual |
| Change the plan, reassign, or ask for status | Tell the **main bot in its own topic**; it forwards the message into the right child topic |

Tip: a child bot's session lives only in its own child topic. When the main bot talks to a child bot, the message also goes into that child topic, never as an @ in the main group (an @ there would just start a new session with no context).

## Task-tree card (optional, off by default)

When enabled, the main bot posts a **task-tree card** in its own topic on its first dispatch: one row per child topic, showing status, the latest progress line and an "打开话题" (open topic) link. As child topics are picked up, report, finish or fail, the card **updates in place** instead of posting new messages.

Card states (the card itself is shown in Chinese):

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 🔵 在跑 (running) | The child bot is working |
| 🟠 等人 (waiting) | Blocked, someone needs to step in |
| 🟢 已完成 (done) | Sub-project finished |
| 🔴 失败 (failed) | Sub-project failed, the dispatch failed, or the child bot never picked it up |
| ⚪ 已派发 (dispatched) | Sent, not picked up yet |
| ⚫ 已关闭 (closed) | The child topic was closed |

Review child topics carry a "［审查］" (review) tag. The card header can also show a requirement ID and link.

**To enable**: in the Dashboard, go to **Global Settings → General → Multi-topic collaboration** and turn on "Send a task-tree card when dispatching subtasks". "Enable multi-topic collaboration" must be on first.

* Takes effect in about 2 seconds, no restart.
* Sessions running in a sandbox fully follow the new setting from the next new session.
* When off, no card is posted and dispatch behaves exactly as if the feature didn't exist.
* In deployment environments you can set `BOTMUX_DISPATCH_TASK_TREE_CARD_ENABLED=true`; the environment variable wins over the Dashboard setting.

## Turning multi-topic orchestration off

Multi-topic orchestration is **on by default**. If you don't need it, turn off "Enable multi-topic collaboration" under **Global Settings → General → Multi-topic collaboration** in the Dashboard. It applies from the next session, no restart.

When it's off:

* bots no longer get the orchestration skill (`botmux-orchestrate`), so they won't open child topics on their own;
* creating a new sub-project topic is refused;
* appending to an **existing** topic still works, so ordinary bot handoffs are unaffected.

In deployment environments you can also set `BOTMUX_MULTI_TOPIC_ENABLED=false`; the environment variable wins over the Dashboard setting.

## Advanced: command reference

These commands are mostly run by the bots themselves; you rarely type them. For reference or troubleshooting:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `botmux dispatch --title "<title>" --bot-app <appId[:role]> --brief-file <file>` | Open a new sub-project topic and send bots in; repeat `--bot-app` for more bots |
| `botmux dispatch ... --repo <dir>` | Preset the child bot's working directory |
| `botmux dispatch ... --repo <dir> --standby` | Only start the bot in that directory and keep it on standby, no task yet |
| `botmux dispatch --into <topic root message ID> --bot-app <appId> --brief "<text>"` | Append to an existing child topic (follow up, add work, wake a standby bot) |
| `botmux dispatch ... --kind review` | Mark the child topic as a review in the task tree (default is task) |
| `botmux dispatch ... --task-id <id> --task-url <https link>` | Show a requirement ID / link in the task-tree card header |
| `botmux dispatch ... --model <model> --reasoning-effort <level>` | Pick the model and reasoning effort for a new child topic (single bot, new topic only, and the target bot's CLI must support choosing a model) |
| `botmux dispatch tree` | Refresh the task-tree card manually and print a text version; if the feature is off, it just tells you where to enable it |
| `botmux report --status <status> "<progress>"` | A child bot reports progress to the main bot; status is one of `pending` `in_progress` `blocked` `completed` `failed` |

Run `botmux dispatch --help` for all options.

## Advanced: whose identity a dispatch carries

If a bot has per-user authorization on (`triggerUserAuth`, meaning tools like lark-cli run with the personal authorization of whoever sent the current turn), a `--bot-app` dispatch from the main bot passes the **current turn's initiator** along to the child bot. Rules:

* The child bot still checks on its side: whether this person maps to a user of its own app, is in the group, and has authorized the tool.
* Only the current turn started by a real person can carry an identity. If that turn has already ended, a dispatch that needs the identity is refused (error code `dispatch_turn_unproven`) rather than quietly sent without one.
* The session Owner or an earlier sender never stands in for the current initiator, and ordinary bot messages never gain human permissions this way.
* To let a child bot create a scheduled task for someone, add `--delegate schedule:create`, and the host policy must allow it; see [scheduled tasks](/botmux/en/schedule.md).

> Related: [multi-bot collaboration](/botmux/en/multi-bot.md) is its foundation; use [roles and teams](/botmux/en/roles.md) to give bots roles (who writes, who reviews).



---
url: /botmux/en/oncall.md
---

# On-Call Mode

<video src="../img/video-v6-oncall-voice-en.mp4" controls preload="metadata" style="width:100%;border-radius:8px"></video>

Add a bot to a duty, alert, or Q\&A group and bind it to a project directory. From then on **anyone in the group** can @ it with a question. No repo picker, no access request: the bot answers from that directory.

It fits groups where "lots of people ask, at any time, about the same project": duty groups, alert groups, cross-team Q\&A groups.

> **Adding the bot to a group does not open it up.** Everyone in the group can talk to it only after an on-call binding (or after a bare `/grant` opens the whole group). Without either, a non-listed member who @-mentions it is blocked and gets a grant request card. See [Permissions & Access · Being added to a group is not authorization](/botmux/en/permissions.md#being-added-to-a-group-is-not-authorization).

## What changes once it's on

| | Before binding | After binding |
|---|---|---|
| Who can @ the bot and chat | Only the owner, admins (`allowedUsers`) and granted users | **Everyone** in the group, including other bots in it |
| Message quota | Guests admitted by grant cards are quota-limited | **Unlimited** |
| Where new topics start | Repo picker card, or the bot's default directory | Straight into the bound directory |
| Who can change session state (`/cd`, `/restart`, `/close`, card buttons) | Owner / admins | Still only owner / admins |

Bindings are **per bot**: in a group with several bots, only the bound one opens up to the group.

## How to turn it on (pick one)

| You want to… | Use |
|---|---|
| Start using it in one group right now | Option 1: send `/oncall bind` in the group |
| Enable it group by group in a web UI | Option 2: Dashboard "Group Management" |
| Have it on automatically in every group the bot joins | Option 3: Dashboard "Bot Config" |

### Option 1: Send a command in the group

@ the bot in the group and send:

```
/oncall bind ~/projects/your-service
```

* Only the @-mentioned bot is bound. Bind several at once: `@bot1 @bot2 /oncall bind <path>`.
* The directory is created if it doesn't exist.
* Requires operate rights (owner / `allowedUsers`).
* From the **next new topic** in this group, the bot starts in this directory.

### Option 2: Per group in Dashboard "Group Management"

1. Open the Dashboard **Group Management** page, find the group, click **Manage**.
2. Switch to the **Bot settings** tab and pick the bot on the left.
3. Under **Oncall Mode**, click **Enable**, fill in the working directory, and click **Save**.

This affects only this bot in this group. The directory must already exist. Turn **Enable** off and save to unbind.

![Oncall Mode under Group Management · Bot settings](/img/oncall-group-manage-bots.png)

### Option 3: Every group via Dashboard "Bot Config"

Open the **Bot Config** page, select the bot, choose **On-call mode** under **Default Working Directory**, fill in a directory, and click **Save**.

That section is a three-way choice:

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| Pick a repo each time (default) | New sessions show the repo picker in Feishu first |
| Fixed default directory | New sessions start in this directory; permissions unchanged |
| **On-call mode** | Groups auto-bind to this directory and chat opens to the whole group |

With On-call mode selected:

* **When auto-binding happens**: the first time the bot receives a message in a group that isn't bound yet, it binds that group to this directory. New and existing groups alike. Binding happens before the permission check, so the first person (or alert bot) to speak doesn't get a grant card.
* **Groups that are already bound are left alone**, whether bound manually or by another bot.
* **A group that was unbound (`/oncall unbind`, or disabled in the Dashboard) is never auto-bound again.** To bind it again, send `/oncall bind <path>` in the group.
* **DMs and other sessions use this directory too**: the bot's new DM and topic sessions start here by default (DMs are not opened to everyone because of this).
* **When you switch back to one of the other two options**, groups that were auto-bound and still point at this directory are unbound together. Groups you bound manually to another directory stay as they are.

The bot card shows "N chats bound now · M chats auto-bound before". "Auto-bound before" is the size of the auto-bind list, not the current binding count: groups that were unbound, or released when switching modes, are counted too, and none of them will be auto-bound again.

![On-call binding counts in Bot Config](/img/oncall-bot-chat-counts-en.png)

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `/oncall bind <path>` | Bind this bot to the directory in this group; if already bound, switch to the new one. Several bots: `@bot1 @bot2 /oncall bind <path>` |
| `/oncall unbind` | Remove this bot's binding in this group; new topics go back to the repo picker |
| `/oncall status` | Show the directory this bot is bound to here (plain `/oncall` does the same) |

* Subcommands also accept Chinese: `绑定`, `解绑`, `状态`.
* All three must be used in a group and need operate rights.
* In DM session groups (groups created automatically from a private chat), the bot writes the binding when it creates the group, and `/oncall` can't change it. Groups created with `/g` aren't affected; `/oncall` works there as usual.
* After binding, `/cd <path>` inside a session changes the directory and stays in on-call mode.

## How permissions are split

* **Chat**: everyone in the group can ask questions, check logs and read code, with no quota. Users on the block list (`blockedUsers`) are still blocked.
* **Management**: changing directory, restarting, closing the session and clicking streaming-card buttons remain owner / admin only, so group members can't accidentally mess up the session.
* **Opening a few low-risk commands to group members**: add them under "canTalk-allowed daemon commands" in Bot Config (`canTalkDaemonCommands` in `bots.json`), e.g. `/status /help`. Commands that change state, like `/cd` and `/restart`, are best left closed.

> An on-call binding **does not restrict file access**. To keep group members away from secrets and other repositories, also enable [File Sandbox](/botmux/en/sandbox.md) allowlist isolation (the working directory stays writable and changes land on the host). To keep changes off your main branch, open the topic in a separate worktree with `/tw`.

## Who the reply @-mentions

In an on-call group, the "Sent to:" line at the bottom of the bot's reply card @-mentions **whoever asked this turn**, so the person who asked gets the notification. If the asker is another bot, it mentions the owner instead, so two bots don't keep pinging each other.

## Pair it with scheduled tasks

In the on-call group, send:

```
/schedule 每天9:00 检查昨天的报警趋势并总结
```

The bot posts a report to the group every day at that time, so someone's watching even when you're not. Scheduled tasks reuse the group's bound directory. See [Scheduled Tasks](/botmux/en/schedule.md) for more formats.

## Editing `bots.json` by hand

Dashboard settings are stored in `bots.json`, which you can also edit directly:

```json
{
  "oncallChats": [
    { "chatId": "oc_xxx", "workingDir": "~/projects/your-service" }
  ],
  "defaultOncall": { "enabled": true, "workingDir": "~/projects/your-service" }
}
```

* `oncallChats`: per-group bindings, each a chat ID plus a directory.
* `defaultOncall`: the "On-call mode" option.
* `defaultOncallAutoboundChats`: the auto-bind list, maintained by botmux; usually no need to edit it.

For other fields see [bots.json configuration](/botmux/en/bots-json.md).

## FAQ

**On-call mode is on, but a group still didn't get auto-bound?**

* The group was unbound before (`/oncall unbind`, or disabled in the Dashboard), or released when switching modes. Send `/oncall bind <path>` in the group.
* The configured directory doesn't exist on the machine, so auto-binding is skipped. Create it first.

**Want the whole group to be able to chat, without changing directory?**
A bare `/grant` opens the whole group. See [Permissions & Access](/botmux/en/permissions.md).



---
url: /botmux/en/permissions.md
---

# Permissions & Authorization

botmux permissions answer just two questions:

| Permission | Meaning | Examples |
|------------|---------|----------|
| **Talk** (canTalk) | Can this person talk to the bot and give it work | @mention the bot with a question, keep chatting in a topic |
| **Operate** (canOperate) | Can this person change the session itself | `/cd`, `/restart`, `/close`, admin buttons on cards |

Most ways of granting access **give talk only**. Operate rights belong to admins (`allowedUsers`) by default.

## Common operations

Start with this table — it covers most needs:

| What you want | How |
|---------------|-----|
| Let **the whole group** ask, no message limit | Send `@bot /grant` (or `/grant all`) in the group. Revoke with a bare `/revoke`. In a topic group it covers every topic |
| Give **specific people** a short trial | `@bot /grant @Alice @Bob` — the bot replies with a grant card, defaulting to 3 messages / 1 hour per person |
| Set the count directly | `@bot /grant @Alice 20` — 20 messages each; the duration is still picked on the card |
| Fine-tune on the card | Duration: **1 hour / 8 hours / 1 day / 7 days / permanent**. Message quota: an integer from 1 to 1000; **leave blank for unlimited**. Whichever runs out first ends the grant |
| Revoke someone's access | `@bot /revoke @Alice` (you can @ several people at once). It removes their per-group and global grants; **if they are also on the `allowedUsers` admin list, that entry is removed too**, and the reply names the affected scopes. Revoking the owner, or a revoke that would leave the bot with no admin, is refused |
| Duty-group instant Q\&A, no repo picking | `/oncall bind ~/projects/foo` — see [On-Call Mode](/botmux/en/oncall.md) |
| Grant in bulk from a web page | Dashboard **Group Management** → the group's **Manage** → **Member access** tab (screenshot below) |

Only owners / admins can run `/grant` and `/revoke`. Granted people (guests) can only talk.

![The Member access tab under Group Management in the Dashboard](/img/permissions-group-member-access.png)

On the **Member access** tab you can:

* **Grant selected**: pick members (up to 50 at a time), with an optional message quota and duration. Membership is re-checked live before anything is written.
* **Whole-chat grant / Revoke whole-chat grant**: same as a bare `/grant` / `/revoke` in the group.
* **Block / Unblock**: add someone to or remove them from the block list, see [Block list](#block-list-blockedusers).
* Grants are written from one bot's point of view. If the group has several bots, pick the bot under **Bot viewpoint** at the top first.

## All the ways to grant access

From "a few people" to "anyone at all":

| Method | Who gets access | Scope | Quota / expiry | Operate | How to turn it on |
|--------|-----------------|-------|----------------|---------|-------------------|
| **Admins** `allowedUsers` | People on the list | Every group and DM of this bot | Long-lived | Talk + operate | `botmux setup`, edit `bots.json`, `/botconfig set allowedUsers` |
| **Guest (this group)** `chatGrants` | Named people (humans or bots) | Only the group it was granted in (all topics in a topic group) | 3 messages / 1 hour by default, adjustable on approval | Talk only | `@bot /grant @someone` grant card; Dashboard Member access; for bots in a group, [`botmux grant chat`](#grant-chat-cli) |
| **Guest (global)** `globalGrants` | Named people | Any group | Same as above | Talk only | **Grant talk globally** on an owner-initiated grant card |
| **Whole group open** `allowedChatGroups` | **Everyone in the group** (leaving revokes it automatically, new members can use it at once) | One group | No quota, no expiry, until revoked | Talk only | Bare `/grant` in the group; Dashboard **Whole-chat grant** |
| **On-call group** | Everyone in the group | One group | Always allowed, never quota-limited | Talk only; new topics go straight to the bound directory, no repo picking | `/oncall bind <dir>`; Dashboard on-call toggle |
| **Open DMs** `p2pOpen` | Everyone inside the Lark app's availability scope | DMs only | — | Talk only | Dashboard **Bot Config**, `bots.json`, `/botconfig set p2pOpen on` |
| **Open mode** | **Anyone** | Everywhere | — | Talk + operate | The fallback when **none** of the lists above is configured; not recommended long-term |

Notes:

* A bot created through normal onboarding always has its owner in `allowedUsers`, so it is **restricted** by default: only listed people can use it.
* Setting only `p2pOpen` without any admin still counts as restricted: groups are not opened, and nobody can run admin actions.
* Same-team bots and platform team members have their own trust rules, see [Roles & Teams](/botmux/en/roles.md). For bots on the same machine, see [Bots on this machine](#bots-on-this-machine-admin-commands-and-delegated-grants-trustsameownerbots) below.
* Guest grants (per group / global), with their quotas and expiry, are kept in a local grant store, `grants.sqlite`, not in `bots.json`. Expired grants are cleaned up automatically every hour. Field details: [bots.json](/botmux/en/bots-json.md#permissions-and-authorization).
* The meeting assistant has a separate, off-by-default switch, **Let inviters manage this meeting** (Dashboard **Global Settings → Meeting Listener → Meeting role presets → Per-bot meeting switches**). It only lets the inviter manage the meeting they invited the assistant to, and grants nothing else on the bot.

## Being added to a group is not authorization

**Pulling the bot into a group does not open up that group.**

* On a **restricted bot** (one with an owner / admin list — every onboarded bot is one), people not on the list are **blocked** when they @mention the bot, and the bot automatically sends the owner a [grant request card](#grant-request-cards). One click from the owner and they're in.
* **Only an open-mode bot with no lists configured at all** can be used by anyone. That is a fallback state, unrelated to being added to a group.
* "Auto-start when added to a group" (`autoStartOnGroupJoin`) is not authorization either. It has its own gate: the group must contain at least one admin before the bot auto-starts a session.

To control who can add the bot to groups, use the Lark developer console (app availability scope, who can add bots to groups).

## Grant request cards

On a restricted bot, when someone without access explicitly @mentions the bot in a group, the bot sends the owner a request card:

* The card has **Grant talk in this chat** and **Deny**; quota and duration can be changed right on the card.
* The card the owner gets from their own `@bot /grant @someone` also has **Grant talk globally** (works in any group).
* After approval, **the message that triggered the request** is fed into the session automatically, so the person doesn't need to resend it.
* Pending cards still work after a daemon restart.
* When the duration or quota runs out, the grant is revoked automatically.

What the requester sees if they message the bot again while waiting:

| Situation | What they see |
|-----------|---------------|
| The card was posted as a reply to their own message | No extra reply — the card itself shows it's waiting for an admin. New messages sent meanwhile are not processed |
| The card was forwarded to the owner's DM (see below) | A one-line "still waiting for the admin" (once per card). That message is not processed; send it again after approval |
| Within 10 minutes of a denial | A one-line "not approved" (once per denial). After 10 minutes, a new message sends a fresh card |

Special cases:

* **Turn off automatic cards**: Dashboard **Bot Config → Authorization & Quota → Auto grant card for blocked @mentions** (`autoGrantRequestCards`, on by default). When off, messages are still blocked, just silently.
* **A blocked DM is silent by default**: there's no owner in that DM, and replying with a card would go to the stranger (useless to them, and it would reveal the owner), so no card is sent.
* **Blocked users** never trigger request cards.

### Forward request cards to the owner's DM

The switch is `grantRequestToOwnerDm`, off by default. Useful when the owner doesn't want to join groups, or people often DM the bot.

When it's on and **no admin in the conversation can click the card**, the card goes to the primary owner's DM instead:

* no admin is found in the group (e.g. **auto-invite owner** `autoInviteOwnerOnGroupAdd` is off and the owner isn't in the group), or
* a DM was blocked.

What happens:

* The requester only gets a neutral acknowledgement that doesn't reveal who the owner is. After the owner approves or denies, the outcome is posted back to the original conversation.
* Once the quota runs out, the next message re-applies automatically.
* If an admin is in the group, or the member lookup fails, the card is posted in the group as before.
* Anti-spam: each owner gets at most 20 forwarded cards per hour (failed sends don't count). Over the cap or on a send failure, no card is sent this time; the next message retries.
* In groups the member list is checked on every request (60-second cache). If the app lacks the member-read scope (`im:chat.members:read`), or the group has more than 2,000 members (no complete list), the card is posted in the group as before.

Turn it on in the Dashboard (**Bot Config → Authorization & Quota → Forward grant requests to the owner's DM**), in `bots.json`, or with `/botconfig set grantRequestToOwnerDm on`.

## Block list `blockedUsers`

The block list is a per-**sender** veto, maintained in the Dashboard **Bot Config**, or directly with **Block** on a group's **Member access** tab.

* Applies to **both groups and DMs**. A blocked person is stopped in on-call groups, whole-group-open groups and team groups alike — switching groups doesn't help.
* Blocked people **don't** trigger request cards to the owner, so you aren't bothered repeatedly.
* **Owners / admins cannot be blocked** — the write is refused, so you can't lock yourself out.
* The block list governs talk only. [Message listeners](/botmux/en/bots-json.md#message-listener) (rules that make a bot watch messages automatically) have their own matching scope and are not affected.

## Advanced: defaults and command permissions

| What you want | Setting | Where |
|---------------|---------|-------|
| Change the grant card's default duration | `grantDefaultDurationMs`: 1 hour / 8 hours / 1 day / 7 days; default 1 hour | Dashboard **Bot Config → Authorization & Quota → Default access duration** |
| Change the grant card's default message count | `messageQuota.defaultLimit`: 1–1000; default 3. Guests only — on-call groups are never metered; `/grant @someone N` still uses N | Same section, **Message quota override** |
| Guests may chat but not use any slash command | `restrictGrantCommands: true`. Only affects people let in by per-group / global guest grants; owners, admins, on-call groups and whole-group-open members are unaffected | Same section, **Restrict grantees to plain conversation**, or `/botconfig set restrictGrantCommands on` |
| Let people with talk access use certain botmux commands | `canTalkDaemonCommands`, e.g. `/status /help`. Only commands botmux handles itself are accepted; typos and passthrough commands are ignored. Be careful opening up state-changing commands like `/cd` or `/restart` | Dashboard **Bot Config → Slash commands → canTalk-allowed daemon commands**, or `/botconfig set canTalkDaemonCommands /status,/help` |

`/grant` and `/revoke` are not affected by `canTalkDaemonCommands`; they always require an admin.

## Bots on this machine: admin commands and delegated grants `trustSameOwnerBots`

"Bots on this machine" means the other bots in the same `bots.json` on the same machine. They can already talk to each other. If the other bot's **owner is the same person as this bot's**, it gets three more abilities (on by default):

* **Talk before it is recognized**: its messages get through, with no grant card, even before this bot has learned who it is — for example when it posts a top-level message in a topic group without @mentioning this bot and this bot has `autoStartOnNewTopic` on. For this reason `botmux create-group` no longer writes pairwise chat grants between same-owner bots on this machine (bots with a different owner still get them).
* **Admin commands**: it can run `/cd`, `/repo`, `/restart`, `/close` and other admin commands on this bot, on par with team bots from other deployments. Commands that only accept the admin list, such as `/botconfig`, `/dashboard` and `/term`, are unaffected.
* **Delegated grants**: when it @mentions this bot in a group, the other people it @mentions in the same message get **talk access in that group**, just like the owner clicking **Grant talk in this chat** (talk only, with the grant card's default quota / duration; `restrictGrantCommands` still applies). A result card is posted under that message, @mentioning the granted humans (other bots are shown by name only, without a notification). People who can already talk, @all, the sender itself and blocked users are skipped; groups only.

How it decides:

* **Is it a bot on this machine**: the union\_id Lark stamps on the message must match exactly one other app in this machine's `bots.json` (`apiOnly` bots excluded). Display names are not used.
* **Same owner**: **every** admin of the other bot must also be an admin of this bot. One extra admin this bot doesn't recognize rules it out — otherwise that person could operate this bot through the other one. The two sides may write admins differently (email, phone number, `on_`, `ou_`); each is converted to a union\_id before comparing, and if any admin can't be converted (e.g. the app lacks contact read permission), it's ruled out too. After an admin change it takes effect again within about 30 seconds.
* Whoever can drive the other bot (its guests, people in its on-call groups) may also drive this bot through it. That's inherent to trust between bots; turn the switch off if that's not acceptable.
* When one machine hosts bots for several people, bots with a different owner can still only talk.

To turn it off: Dashboard **Bot Config → Authorization & Quota → Trust bots on this machine with the same owner**, `trustSameOwnerBots: false` in `bots.json`, or `/botconfig set trustSameOwnerBots off`. When off, every bot on this machine can only talk (picking a repository with `/repo` is not affected). If you turn it off for existing groups, a bot pair that was never recognized has no earlier chat grant to fall back on and needs a new `/grant`.

### Carry the sender over on @ handoffs (`delegateOnMention`) {#delegate-on-mention}

The trust above decides whether bots on this machine may operate each other; this setting decides whose identity the work runs under after a handoff.

When this bot hands work to another bot on the same machine with `botmux send --mention` in **a turn a person started directly**, the receiving bot runs `lark-cli` / `bytedcli` **as that person**, not as itself or as whatever is logged in on the machine.

* **On by default**, but it only takes effect when the handing-off bot itself has [Run CLI calls as the message sender](/botmux/en/bots-json.md#trigger-user-auth) on (`enabled` is `true` and `tools` is not empty): a bot that doesn't run its own tools as the sender has no verified sender to hand over.
* The receiving bot must have that setting on too, and it still checks that this person may talk to it and is in the chat.
* Only between bots on the same machine; bots on other machines never receive it. Handing work out with `botmux dispatch` is not affected by this switch; see [whose identity a dispatch carries](/botmux/en/multi-topic.md#advanced-whose-identity-a-dispatch-carries).
* To turn it off: untick **Hand the sender over on @ handoffs to bots on this machine** under Dashboard **Bot Config → Security → Trigger-user auth**, or add `"delegateOnMention": false` to `triggerUserAuth`. When off, the receiving turn of an @ handoff has no usable sender.

## Grant-delegate bots `grantDelegateBots`

This is the **second delegation source** besides same-owner bots on this machine: a list of external bots the owner explicitly trusts. The two don't affect each other. The delegated grant works exactly as in the previous section — only "who counts as a delegate" differs.

Typical case: an external platform creates a group with its own bot and posts a kickoff card that @mentions this bot and the person making the request. In restricted mode that person is blocked when they @mention this bot and must wait for the owner's approval. Adding the platform bot to the list removes that step.

* Entries are the trusted bot's open\_id as seen by this bot (`ou_…`) or its app\_id (`cli_…`).
* When a listed bot **@mentions this bot** in a group, everyone else it @mentions in the same message gets **talk access in that group**: talk only, with the grant card's default quota / duration; `restrictGrantCommands` still applies.
* A result card is posted under that message, @mentioning the granted humans (other bots are shown by name only, to avoid waking them).
* Skipped: people who can already talk, the sender itself, @all, blocked users; never in DMs. A delegate bot that is itself blocked is ignored entirely.
* **Trust boundary**: this hands the listed bots the power to pick who can talk to this bot in a group. They can't grant operate rights, can't change `allowedUsers` / `allowedChatGroups` / `globalGrants`, and the grant only covers the group the message was posted in. List only platform bots you fully trust.
* The list is empty by default, which behaves the same as not configuring it.

Configure it in the Dashboard (**Bot Config → Authorization & Quota → External bots with delegated grants**), via `grantDelegateBots` in `bots.json`, or with `/botconfig set grantDelegateBots ou_xxx,cli_yyy` (`/botconfig unset grantDelegateBots` clears it).

## Grant a bot in a group from the command line `botmux grant chat` {#grant-chat-cli}

To let a bot talk to a bot on this machine in **one specific group** from a script, use `botmux grant chat`. It only writes a this-group guest grant (`chatGrants`) and gives talk only.

```bash
# Recommended: pass the other bot's App ID; the receiver resolves its own open_id for it
botmux grant chat --bot <receiver> --chat-id oc_xxx --subject-bot cli_xxx

# If you already know the open_id as seen by the receiver
botmux grant chat --bot <receiver> --chat-id oc_xxx --subject-open-id ou_xxx

# Revoke
botmux grant chat revoke --bot <receiver> --chat-id oc_xxx --subject-open-id ou_xxx

# Check whether a grant exists
botmux grant chat readback --bot <receiver> --chat-id oc_xxx --subject-open-id ou_xxx
```

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--bot` | The receiver: the bot on this machine that will accept messages from the subject. Use the full App ID, display name, or a unique cliId; ambiguous refs are rejected. Its daemon must be online |
| `--chat-id` | The group's `oc_…` ID; exactly one |
| `--subject-bot` | The granted bot's App ID (`cli_…`); repeatable. **Grant only** |
| `--subject-open-id` | The granted bot's `ou_…` as seen by the receiver; repeatable |

Key points:

* Use either `--subject-bot` or `--subject-open-id`, not both. Up to 50 subjects at once.
* **Grant** checks the group's bot members live. Every subject must be a bot currently in the group; if any one isn't, the whole batch is rejected and nothing is written. If the lookup fails, the grant is rejected too, with no fallback to past records.
* **Revoke** doesn't check membership, so you can still clean up a grant after the bot has left. Revoke and readback only accept `--subject-open-id`.
* **Readback** only answers for the subjects you ask about; it never lists all grants.
* Grants made with this command have **no message limit and no expiry** until revoked. If the subject had a quota or duration before, granting again makes it unlimited.
* It doesn't change `allowedUsers`, `allowedChatGroups`, or team trust, and doesn't grant admin commands such as `/repo`, `/cd`, `/restart`.
* Run it on the machine where the daemon runs; the command reads the local `.dashboard-secret` to call the receiver daemon.
* On success it prints one line of JSON to stdout; on failure it prints the error to stderr and exits non-zero.

## Common questions

* **On-call vs bare `/grant`?** Both give talk only. On-call also binds the group to a working directory so new topics skip repo picking; `/grant` only opens talk.
* **How do I give someone exactly 3 messages?** The card from `@bot /grant @someone` defaults to 3 messages / 1 hour; you can also add a number after the mention or change it on the card.
* **Does every new member need owner approval?** No. With whole-group open (bare `/grant`) or on-call, anyone in the group can use the bot right away. Per-person grants and request cards are for when you want to keep the gate.
* **A granted person's messages get no response?** First check whether their quota or duration has run out; then check whether `restrictGrantCommands` is on and they sent a slash command.

For more Q\&A see the [FAQ / Troubleshooting](/botmux/en/faq.md); for when you must @mention the bot, see [@ Policy](/botmux/en/mention-mode.md).
