The order is always: **group role > default role > none**. For example, the same bot can be a "strict code reviewer" in group A, a "patient Q\&A helper" in group B, and use its default role everywhere else.

### With commands in the group

@-mention the bot in the group and send:

| Command | Effect |
|------|------|
| `/role` | Show the persona in effect and where it comes from (group / default) |
| `/role set <Markdown>` | Set the group role; multi-line is fine |
| `/role delete` | Delete the group role and fall back to the default role |
| `/role team` | Show the default role |
| `/role team set <Markdown>` | Set the default role (the command keeps the old name `team`; it means "default role") |
| `/role team delete` | Delete the default role |

Example:

```text
/role set You are this group's technical advisor.
- Give the conclusion first, then the reasoning
- Flag risks before any production change
```

* Personas are written in Markdown and injected into the CLI as a `<role>` block.
* Each persona can be up to 32 KB (about 10,000 CJK characters); anything beyond that is truncated.
* After a change, "every turn" mode picks it up from the next message; "only once" mode picks it up on a new or rebuilt session (see [Per-group switches](#per-group-switches)).

### In the Dashboard

If you'd rather not type commands, open `botmux dashboard`:

| What to change | Where |
|------|------|
| Default role | **Bot Config** page, each bot's "**Default Role**" section (same config as `/role team set`; saving it empty deletes it) |
| Group role | **Role Management** page → "By Group": expand a group, pick a bot, edit |
| Jump there from a group | **Group Management** page: in a bot's settings for that group, click "Edit chat role" |

![Dashboard Bot Config — Default Role editor](https://magic-builder.tos-cn-beijing.volces.com/uploads/1780051089378_default-role-shot.png)

When you use "Duplicate" on the Group Management page to copy a group, you can tick "Also copy chat roles" to carry the source group's group roles (plus the per-group switches below) into the new group. Default roles are inherited automatically, so they don't need copying.

## Per-group switches

On the **Role Management** page, select a bot in a group. Besides editing the persona, you can set the options below. Each is saved per "group + bot" and takes effect immediately.

| Switch | Default | What it does |
|------|------|------|
| **Injection** | Every turn | "Every turn" sends the persona with every message; "Only once (first turn)" injects it only when a session starts or is rebuilt, which suits long personas and saves tokens. You can change the default per bot in the "Default Role" section of the Bot Config page, then override it for individual groups |
| **Prefer private replies to the requester** | Off | When on, the answer is sent to the asker in a private chat first; if that fails, it's posted publicly in the original topic. You can also set a "Group notice" (e.g. "Sent to you privately to avoid noise") shown in the original topic after a successful private reply; leave it empty for no notice |
| **Topic task reporting mode** | Off | See below |

**Topic task reporting mode**: when this bot uses `botmux dispatch` in this group to hand a task to another bot, the assignee still uses `botmux report` to hand the result back to the dispatcher's session. With this switch on, the assignee also posts "completion + output location/summary" with `botmux send --no-mention` in the topic where it received the task, so people can see the result right in the group. It doesn't mention the dispatcher or open a new topic. `--standby` (reserve a bot without sending a task) doesn't involve this step.

> In project groups, the coordinator bot also receives Botmux's fixed project-state protocol (for tracking progress and the pinned project card). It applies alongside the Role and is not affected by the Role's injection mode. For project groups, see `/project` in [Slash Commands](/botmux/en/slash-commands.md).

## Role profiles

A profile is a **reusable bundle of group roles**: write a persona for each of several bots, save them under a name (e.g. `collab-main`), and apply them to a new group in one step later.

It's only a shortcut for writing: once applied, it becomes an ordinary group role. It doesn't add another persona layer and doesn't support template inheritance.

### Commands

| Command | Effect |
|------|------|
| `/role profile list` | List all profiles and show whether the current bot has its own entry |
| `/role profile show <name>` | Show the current bot's persona in that profile; add `--all` to see every bot's |
| `/role profile set <name> <Markdown>` | Write the current bot's entry directly |
| `/role profile save <name>` | Save the current bot's effective persona (group role, or the default role if there's none) into the profile |
| `/role profile delete <name>` | Delete the current bot's entry |
| `/role profile apply <name>` | Write the current bot's entry as the group role |

Flags for `apply`:

* `--preview`: preview only, write nothing.
* `--force`: if the group already has a role, apply refuses by default; add this to overwrite.
* `--quiet`: no reply on success (less noise when applying in bulk).

Notes:

* Each bot only manages its own entry and never changes another bot's persona.
* If the profile has no entry for the current bot, `apply` writes nothing and the bot keeps using its default role.
* Profile names may only use letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-`, up to 64 characters.

### In the Dashboard

**Role Management** page → "Profiles" tab:

1. Open or create a profile on the left.
2. In the middle, see which bots have entries; select a bot to edit its persona.
3. Under "Apply To Group", choose the target group and the bots to apply. Click **Preview Apply** first to check whether existing roles would be overwritten, then **Apply Profile**. Tick "Overwrite existing group roles" when you do want to overwrite.

### Apply while creating a group

```text
@botA @botB @botC /g --role-profile collab-main War Room
```

Once the new group exists, the bot that created it applies its own entry, then posts `@botB @botC /role profile apply collab-main --quiet` in the new group so the other bots apply their own entries.

## Capability tags

A capability tag is a one-line self-introduction, such as "Good at frontend and UI review". It helps you and other bots pick the right one when collaborating.

```text
/role cap set Good at frontend and UI review   # set
/role cap                                      # show
/role cap clear                                # clear
```

* Tags are capped at 120 characters. One sentence is enough; use `/role set` for a full persona.
* When other bots run `botmux bots list` to see who's in the group, they see each bot's tag.
* Tip: put `workspace: required` / `optional` / `none` in the tag so dispatching bots know whether they must specify a repo or working directory when giving you a task.

Personas plus capability tags are the foundation of [multi-bot collaboration](/botmux/en/multi-bot.md): with clear identities and responsibilities, bots are less likely to get mixed up when @-mentioned in a group.

## Teams: collaborating across machines

The Dashboard used to have a "Team" page; it has been removed. To work with bots on **other people's machines**, your machine needs to be connected to the central platform and be in the same team. Then use the command line:

* `botmux bots list --scope team`: list bots that have joined your team.
* `botmux create-group --team <team> --agent <appId>`: pull them and their owners into a new group.

Full steps are in the "Team scope" section of [Multi-Bot Collaboration](/botmux/en/multi-bot.md).

## Role switch (advanced)

> ⚠️ Advanced feature: you need to deploy a "role library" first, and it currently supports Claude Code only. Deployment steps are in the repo's [role-system deploy runbook](https://github.com/deepcoldy/botmux/blob/master/docs/roles/deploy-runbook.md). Below is how to use it once deployed.

`/role` above means "one persona per bot". **Role switch** gives one bot **several full roles**, each with its own persona and **its own memory**. Switch to "After-sales" and it carries the after-sales persona and experience that belongs only to after-sales; switch to "Product manager" and it's a different set.

Roles apply **per topic**; a new topic starts from the default role.

### How to use it: just talk

| You say | What the bot does |
|------|-----------|
| "switch role" / "what roles are there" | Lists the roles you can use (shared ones + ones you created), numbered for you to pick |
| "switch to After-sales" or reply with a number | Confirms and switches; from then on this topic is answered by that role, and the card footer shows the role name |
| "new role: Xiaohongshu ops, familiar with our brand voice" | Drafts a persona for you to confirm, then creates it and switches to it |
| "distill knowledge" | Turns the role's recent memory into structured knowledge stored back in the role (optionally as a Lark doc for human review) |

Behind the scenes the model runs `botmux role switch <role-dir>`; you don't need to type it yourself.

### Good to know

* **Separate memory**: each role has one memory, shared across groups and topics, so it gets better at its domain the more it's used.
* **Context is kept**: switching restarts the CLI and resumes the previous conversation; the new role's persona and memory load automatically when the new session starts.
* **Private roles are not a security boundary**: "you only see shared roles and your own" is a convention in the role protocol file (`_role-protocol.md`) that the model follows. The daemon enforces only one thing: the target directory must be inside the role library `~/botmux-roles`. It does not isolate roles per sender. If you need real isolation, add OS-level permissions yourself.
* **Not the same as `/cd`**: `/cd <path>` (see [Slash Commands](/botmux/en/slash-commands.md)) is the general "change working directory and restart", works with any directory, and needs operate permission. Role switch only moves within the role library.

> The old command `botmux cd` has been renamed to `botmux role switch`. The old name now only prints an error and does not switch. When maintaining an older deployment, update `_role-protocol.md` in the role library to the new command.



---
url: /botmux/en/sandbox.md
---

# File & Network Sandbox

The sandbox limits what the CLI behind a bot can touch on your host: it keeps secrets out of reach and stops the CLI from wrecking your environment. It is configured per bot and **works on both Linux and macOS**.

## Pick a mode

The file sandbox is one switch with three positions:

| Mode (config value) | In one line | What it can read | Where writes go | Who it suits |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Off (`off`, the default) | No isolation | Every host file | Straight to the host | Only you, in a fully trusted environment |
| Allowlist isolation (`oncall`) | **Keep secrets in** | Only allowlisted paths; everything else does not exist inside the sandbox | Writable allowlisted paths, written straight to the host | Sharing the bot with group members or outside collaborators |
| scratch (`scratch`) | **Keep the machine clean** | The whole real filesystem (only botmux's own credentials are hidden) | A throwaway copy, discarded when the session ends; the host is untouched | Your own risky commands, experimental refactors, building untrusted code |

How to choose:

* **Other people will use this bot** (group members, Oncall, several authorized users) → choose **Allowlist isolation**. Private keys, tokens, other repositories and other bots' data are invisible by default.
* **Only you use it, but you worry a command will mess up the machine** → choose **scratch**. No allowlist to configure, every tool just works, and anything that breaks is simply thrown away.
* ⚠️ **scratch isolates writes, not credentials**: the agent can still read the secrets on this machine, including other people's tokens and login state (such as `user-token-*` and `lark-cli-home/` under `~/.botmux/data/`). Do not use scratch for a bot several people share.

> The sandbox governs which files the CLI can access, not who can talk to the bot. Who can talk is decided by [On-Call Mode](/botmux/en/oncall.md) and [Permissions](/botmux/en/permissions.md).

## Turning it on

### In the Dashboard (recommended)

1. Open the Dashboard → **Bot Config** → select the bot.
2. Under **File sandbox**, pick **Off / Allowlist isolation / scratch (throwaway)**.
3. When switching to Allowlist isolation or scratch, a confirmation dialog explains what the mode does; click **Switch**. Switching back to Off has no dialog.
4. For scratch you can also pick the storage: in-memory or disk.

The Dashboard also checks a few things for you:

* When the bot is used by more than its owner (Oncall, whole-group access, several `allowedUsers`, or per-sender auth) but allowlist isolation is off, it suggests turning it on and says whether the current CLI is verified to work.
* When you pick scratch, it warns up front if this machine cannot run scratch or can only use disk storage, and lists the missing dependencies and how to install them.

### In `bots.json`

```json
[
  {
    "name": "public-oncall",
    "cliId": "codex",
    "sandbox": "oncall",
    "sandboxPaths": { "deny": ["~/.kube"] }
  },
  {
    "name": "my-scratch",
    "cliId": "claude-code",
    "sandbox": "scratch",
    "scratchStorage": "tmpfs"
  }
]
```

* Leaving out `sandbox`, or setting it to `false`, means off; `true` is the same as `"oncall"`.
* The legacy field `readIsolation: true` is treated as allowlist isolation and migrated automatically at daemon startup.

### When changes take effect

**New sessions only.** A session records its sandbox mode the first time it starts and keeps using that record. Running sessions keep the mode they started with, even across `/restart` or a daemon restart. To use the new mode right away, start a new topic.

To check whether a session is sandboxed:

* The session card in Lark shows a small line "🛡️ Sandbox: Allowlist isolation" or "🛡️ Sandbox: scratch (throwaway)". No line means no sandbox.
* In the Dashboard session list and kanban, a session whose recorded sandbox mode differs from the bot's current config is tagged "Sandbox ≠ config". Hover to see both values (for example "session uses Off, config is now Allowlist isolation").

"Sandbox ≠ config" is not an error. It means you changed this bot's sandbox mode after the session started, and the session still runs with the old mode.

| You want | Do this |
|---|---|
| This session to use the new mode | Start a new topic. `/restart` does not switch the mode, and the tag stays |
| To keep the old mode | Nothing. The session keeps working as before |

Sessions that have not started yet (for example, still picking a repo) don't show this tag.

### Forcing it on machine-wide

`BOTMUX_SANDBOX` is handy for testing or blanket hardening and applies to every bot on the machine:

| Value | Effect |
|---|---|
| `1` or `oncall` | Every bot is forced into allowlist isolation |
| `scratch` | Every bot is forced into scratch |
| Unset, empty, `0`, `false` | No force; each bot follows its own `sandbox` setting |
| Anything else | Rejected at startup |

The variable **can only force the sandbox on, never off**: setting it to `0` does not turn off a sandbox the bot enables itself.

***

## Allowlist isolation (`oncall`)

The CLI is confined to a per-session file allowlist that governs both reads and writes. However group members try to steer the model, it cannot reach your private keys, other repositories, or Lark app secrets. It is often paired with [On-Call Mode](/botmux/en/oncall.md).

### What the sandbox can see

| Path | Inside the sandbox |
|---|---|
| Working directory (`workingDir`) | Read-write; changes land on the host directly |
| System tools, shared libraries, the CLI itself | Read-only |
| `/tmp`, `/run`, `/var/tmp`, `/dev/shm` | Session-private empty directories, separate from the host |
| `~/.ssh`, `~/.aws`, shared `~/.lark-cli` | Hidden |
| `~/.botmux` (botmux data directory) | Only what this session needs (the bot's own `bots/<appId>/`, the `botmux` command and plugins, this session's records); `bots.json`, the Dashboard secret and other bots' directories can be neither read nor written |
| botmux install directory | Read-only, so the `botmux` command runs; if it is a git checkout, files git does not track (`.env`, login state, `data/`, …) and `.git` are hidden |
| Rest of your home directory | **Not mounted as a whole**, unless it is inside the working directory |
| Network | **Not restricted** by default, same as the host; see [Network sandbox](#network-sandbox) |

Things to watch:

* **Point the working directory at a specific project** (e.g. `~/proj`). `workingDir` defaults to `~`, which puts every unhidden file in your home directory on the allowlist, writable.
* The working directory cannot be inside the botmux data directory (except the bot's own `bots/<appId>/`); such a session refuses to start.
* On Linux, the private `/run` also holds a few read-only mounts the session needs: the command relay directory `/run/sbxbin`, the MCP plugin gateway socket directory (when the gateway is on), `/etc/resolv.conf` when it links into `/run`, and CLI / interpreter directories living under `/run` (such as fnm or nvm multishell directories).

### Adding paths or masks (`sandboxPaths`)

To let the sandbox see more directories, or hide more sensitive paths:

```jsonc
{
  "sandbox": "oncall",
  "sandboxPaths": {
    // Extra read-write directories
    "readWrite": ["~/shared-output"],
    // Extra read-only directories (shared sources, docs, …)
    "readOnly": ["/srv/shared-libs", "~/docs/runbooks"],
    // Extra sensitive paths to hide
    "deny": ["~/.kube", "/opt/confidential"]
  }
}
```

Rules:

* **Use absolute paths** (starting with `/` or `~/`). A relative path is resolved against the session working directory, where `..` may already be your home directory, so none of the three lists accepts one.
* **`readWrite` cannot contain `/`, your home directory, the botmux data directory, or any parent of them**: that would hand the whole disk or every credential to the sandbox. A specific directory such as `~/projects/foo` is fine.
* **On Linux, `readOnly` cannot contain `/` or `/run`**: the mount points the sandbox needs could not be created and the session would exit at launch. Use specific directories such as `/usr`, `/opt/<tool dir>`, `/run/lock`.
* The Dashboard rejects these on save and explains why. Older entries hand-written into `bots.json` are downgraded at spawn: home / data directory move from read-write to read-only, `/` and relative paths in `readWrite` are dropped, and on Linux `/` and `/run` in `readOnly` are dropped too.
* `readWrite` / `readOnly` paths that do not exist yet are skipped at spawn; to allow a file that has not been created, allow its existing parent directory.
* The legacy fields `sandboxHidePaths` and `sandboxReadonlyPaths` are still read and are migrated to `deny` / `readOnly` at daemon startup.

### Where each CLI keeps its data

* **Claude Code (including Seed, built on it) and Codex**: config, transcripts and memory live in the bot's own directory `<BOTMUX_HOME>/bots/<appId>/` (`.../claude`, `.../codex`) instead of your global `~/.claude` / `~/.codex`. The Dashboard shows "Enhanced CLI data isolation".
* **Other CLIs** (Cursor, Antigravity, Grok, Kimi, …): keep using their global data directory on the host, mounted into the sandbox as each adapter declares (some writable as a whole directory, some only their credential files).
* With `wrapperCli` configured, this redirect is skipped and the CLI uses its usual data directory.

### Which CLIs are verified

These CLIs were tested under allowlist isolation on Linux (start, first turn, shell tool, working directory read/write, network, `botmux send` and credential isolation, on both tmux and pty backends):

Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, OpenCode, Pi, oh-my-pi, Grok, Kimi.

* **Codex App** does not support allowlist isolation on Linux and refuses to start; use Codex instead.
* Other CLIs have not been verified one by one; try one in a test session first.

### Using it with `wrapperCli`

A bot with a launch prefix (`wrapperCli`) can also be sandboxed (pty / tmux backends). The wrapper itself runs inside the sandbox, under the same allowlist:

* botmux only lets in the wrapper's own executable file and the CLI it calls.
* Anything else the wrapper needs (its install tree, interpreter, config) must be added to `sandboxPaths`: `readOnly` for reading, `readWrite` if it writes.
* When a path is missing, the session names it before starting; if the wrapper exits right after launch, the topic also suggests adding the paths to `sandboxPaths`. Under scratch it suggests checking `scratchDenyPaths` instead.

### Multiple accounts & credentials

* **Codex isolated login (`codexAuthSync: "isolated"`)**: points `CODEX_HOME` at `<BOTMUX_HOME>/bots/<appId>/codex` and never reads or touches the global `~/.codex`. Works with the sandbox off or in allowlist isolation; it **cannot be combined with `scratch` or `wrapperCli`** (the session refuses to start). When a session is bound to a non-legacy Codex instance, the instance's own auth mode applies.
* **Codex `config.toml`**: when Codex uses the bot's own directory (allowlist isolation, or `codexAuthSync: "isolated"`; not under scratch or with `wrapperCli`), the `config.toml` in it is copied once from the host's `~/.codex/config.toml` when the first new session starts; later host edits are not synced. The Dashboard (next to "Codex login credentials") shows the path and offers **Re-sync from host** (the current file is backed up as `config.toml.bak-<time>` first), effective for the next new session.
* **Claude per-bot accounts (`credentialsSourceDir`)**: a sandboxed bot takes its OAuth credentials from this directory on every cold start, so sandboxed bots never share an account by accident. No effect on bots without a sandbox; cannot be combined with `codexAuthSync: "isolated"`.
* **lark-cli**: the sandbox hides the shared `~/.lark-cli`. To use lark-cli inside the sandbox, the machine must first split lark-cli config per bot; see [lark-cli per-bot config](https://github.com/deepcoldy/botmux/blob/master/docs/lark-cli-per-bot.md) (Chinese).

#### Several accounts on one machine: a separate account for a Claude bot {#credentials-source-dir}

By default every sandboxed bot on a machine takes its credentials from the shared login (`~/.claude/.credentials.json` or the keychain), so they all run as one Claude account. To give one bot a different account:

1. Prepare an account directory with one sub-directory per CLI, for example:

   ```text
   ~/accounts/acct-b/
   └── claude/
       └── .credentials.json
   ```

2. Set `credentialsSourceDir` for the bot: `"credentialsSourceDir": "~/accounts/acct-b"` in `bots.json`, or send `/botconfig set credentialsSourceDir ~/accounts/acct-b` in Lark.

3. It takes effect for new sessions (`/restart` an existing one). From then on, every cold start copies the credentials from that directory into the bot's own data directory.

Limits:

* **Only `claude-code` is supported for now**, and the bot must have the file sandbox on. On a bot with no sandbox at all it has no effect (the global login is still used and a warning is logged); with the sandbox on but the data directory not redirectable (for example with `wrapperCli`), the session refuses to start.
* If the source directory is missing, unreadable or holds invalid credentials, the session **refuses to start** instead of quietly falling back to the shared login.
* Cannot be combined with `codexAuthSync: "isolated"`. For separate Codex accounts use `codexAuthSync: "isolated"`, see the item above.
* botmux only copies on cold start and **does not refresh** the tokens in the source directory; keeping them valid is up to you (or an external script).
* `/botconfig unset credentialsSourceDir` goes back to the shared login.

***

## scratch (throwaway sandbox)

A disposable environment for your own use.

### How it works

* **Reads: zero setup**. The bot sees the full real filesystem; compilers, global npm / pip packages, `~/.gitconfig` and project configs just work.
* **Writes: all go to a copy**. Editing `/etc`, installing global packages, changing your home directory or project files: every write lands in a separate copy-on-write layer that is discarded when the session ends.
* **Linux**: based on overlayfs, with **zero writes to the host disk**. A root daemon uses kernel overlayfs; a non-root daemon falls back to `fuse-overlayfs` automatically. Separately mounted data disks (such as `/data00`): under root each gets its own copy layer; under non-root they are read-only inside the sandbox, so **keep the working directory on the root filesystem**, otherwise the session refuses to start.
* **macOS**: uses APFS clones of your home directory and project (only changed blocks take space), with system paths read-only. But `~/Library/{Caches,Application Support,Logs}` and system temp dirs such as `/private/tmp` and `/private/var/folders` **still write to the real disk** and are outside the throwaway guarantee.

### Storage and options

```jsonc
{
  "sandbox": "scratch",
  // tmpfs (default, in memory) or disk
  "scratchStorage": "tmpfs",
  // tmpfs size limit in MB; 0 = kernel default, roughly half of RAM
  "scratchTmpfsSizeMb": 4096,
  // Extra paths to hide (botmux's own credentials are hidden by default)
  "scratchDenyPaths": ["~/.ssh"]
}
```

| Storage | Behavior | Requirement |
|---|---|---|
| `tmpfs` in-memory (default) | Kept in RAM, wiped when the session closes or the machine reboots | On Linux, **the daemon must run as root**; use `disk` otherwise |
| `disk` | Kept on disk, survives daemon restarts; cleaned up when the session closes normally | None |

macOS always uses APFS clones; there is no memory / disk choice.

***

## Network sandbox

The file sandbox **does not restrict networking by default**: network and proxy access inside the sandbox are the same as on the host. To restrict it, add one of the following.

### Block all network (`sandboxNetwork: false`)

```jsonc
"sandboxNetwork": false
```

The CLI runs in a network namespace with no outside access. Good for purely local, offline tasks.

### Allow by destination IP (`sandboxNetworkPolicy`)

Use this when the sandbox should reach only certain internal APIs or a proxy. **Linux + pty backend + allowlist isolation only.**

```json
{
  "sandbox": "oncall",
  "backendType": "pty",
  "sandboxNetworkPolicy": {
    "version": 1,
    "public": { "mode": "allow" },
    "private": {
      "mode": "allowlist",
      "rules": [{ "cidr": "10.20.0.0/16", "protocol": "tcp", "ports": [443] }]
    },
    "dnsServers": ["1.1.1.1"]
  }
}
```

* Public (`public`) and private (`private`) ranges are set separately; each can be `allow` (everything), `block` (nothing), `allowlist` (only matching rules) or `denylist` (everything except matching rules).
* Rules use IP / CIDR only and can be limited to TCP / UDP ports; domain names are not supported.
* Filtering happens in the kernel (nftables + slirp4netns) on the real destination IP of each packet.
* In the Dashboard: **Bot Config** → **Destination IP network policy**; edit and click **Save policy**, or **Clear network policy** to remove it.
* **Trusted Proxy Egress (`proxyMode: "trusted-egress"`)**: Ordinary sessions may explicitly delegate proxied business destinations to a trusted exit; the proxy socket itself remains subject to destination IP and port rules.

**Check two things first**, otherwise sessions either start without network access or do not start at all:

1. **Set `dnsServers` explicitly.** With a policy, the sandbox's `/etc/resolv.conf` contains only the `dnsServers` addresses and slirp4netns' built-in DNS forwarder is disabled. Without them there is no DNS and every lookup fails (`getaddrinfo EAI_AGAIN`) — an allow-all policy included. Use the nameservers from the host's `/etc/resolv.conf` (with systemd-resolved that file says `127.0.0.53`, which the sandbox cannot reach; use the upstream servers in `/run/systemd/resolve/resolv.conf`). Only port 53 is opened to them, even inside a blocked `private` zone. The Dashboard's starting template fills in the host's current nameservers.
2. **Choose a trusted exit explicitly for ordinary proxy sessions.** If the daemon or the bot's `env` sets `HTTP_PROXY` / `HTTPS_PROXY` / `ALL_PROXY` (any case), a policy that is not allow-all refuses to start sessions: the proxy resolves and forwards destinations, so the kernel rules only see the proxy. Once the exit is trusted, add `"proxyMode": "trusted-egress"` and permit the proxy's TCP addresses and ports, or remove the proxy variables. Launch validation resolves every proxy endpoint's complete A/AAAA list and refuses any address rejected by zone rules or ordered drops, any port or protocol mismatch, missing or invalid DNS answers, and invalid URLs. Loopback and network gateway aliases cannot be proxy exits. Validation neither rewrites environment variables nor widens kernel rules; the proxy's ACL remains responsible for destinations behind it.

When a plugin freezes a **protected HTTP egress policy** into a session, only the `codex` CLI currently supports the protected model bridge; other CLIs are rejected before launch. This mode cannot be combined with general `proxyMode: "trusted-egress"` delegation or task proxy variables. Conflicts fail explicitly: remove task proxies, clear general proxy delegation, and use the protected model bridge for model connections. The bridge forwards authorized model service connections only; it is not a general HTTP/CONNECT proxy. Direct connections to protected destinations are denied by their frozen IPs and ports within the existing policy; other destinations continue following their existing rules.

Authentication tokens live in the separate `egress-private` subtree of the socket directory (0700 directory, 0600 file). The task's file sandbox masks both `/run/botmux-mcp/egress-private` and its canonical host path. Model and declared local-service bridges read tokens outside the file sandbox; tasks only see the sockets. The runner must install nft rules successfully before readiness, bridges, or task execution. Failure exits instead of using a policy-presence boolean or unused environment flag as proof. Decision logs and unregistered-mutating-candidate warnings omit queries, request headers and bodies.

Shared business reads use `BOTMUX_PROTECTED_EGRESS_PROTOCOL=shared-read-v1`, injected by the sandbox alongside the socket. A supporting CLI keeps the host's existing business login credentials without reading the guard token. The `x-botmux-egress-client: shared-read-v1` marker selects a shared exit, not a user identity or write authorization. The guard must explicitly enable this protocol, still validates the frozen policy and target, and blocks writes registered in `denyRoutes`. POST queries work without a separate read-operation registry. Internal Botmux headers are stripped from business requests; shared requests carrying an authentication token or any `x-botmux-loopback-*` header are rejected and cannot reach host identity services through this exit. Existing model and controlled Lark identity bridges retain private token authentication. Protected writes must still go through the plugin's per-call checks of the current human principal and capability, never the shared business identity.

Deploy the protocol to both Botmux and the calling CLI. Persistent older CLIs may retain their original startup environment; start a new topic after installation and restart. Unknown protocols or missing required sockets must fail without falling back to a direct protected-target connection. Non-Botmux use and requests to other targets keep their original behavior.

`denyRoutes` also denies case-equivalent protected paths. Pathnames reject percent encoding, matrix semicolons, whitespace, duplicate separators and dot paths; no safe encoding allowlist currently exists. Valid pathnames and queries are forwarded unchanged, so legitimate reads need no per-operation registry. Unregistered mutating candidates are still allowed with a warning; the write-route registry must remain complete.

**Residual boundary risk:** Only the finite frozen IPs/ports are denied directly; other private troubleshooting destinations remain direct, without default-block egress. Other A/AAAA answers, CDN edges and unfrozen alternative addresses can still bypass the guard. This is not complete hostname isolation or proof that every write bypass is eliminated. For absolute bypass prevention, do NOT use default block today (block accepts no exception rules, and the protected model bridge exists only when the model host itself is a protected target, so a separate model gateway would become unreachable). Configure the public zone as an allowlist with a sole exit: list required addresses such as the model host explicitly, or rely on a provably complete service/network authorization boundary. Upstreams currently use only `frozenAddresses[0]` without multi-address failover; never blindly retry a possibly executed write.

Close cleans its own authentication file and preserves a stable-path token already rotated by a successor. Cross-process rotation between comparison and unlink still has an availability race, without atomic conditional deletion. Serialize overlapping cross-process startup/teardown for the same session; further protocol hardening remains a follow-up.

Other limits:

* The host `PATH` needs `slirp4netns` (with `--disable-host-loopback` and `--disable-dns`), `nft`, `ip` and `unshare` (with `--kill-child` and `--mount-proc`), and bwrap must support `--add-seccomp-fd` and `--disable-userns`. Nothing is installed automatically; if any piece is missing, the session refuses to start.
* A bot without its own backend setting uses the daemon default (tmux); switch it to pty under "Session backend" in the Dashboard.
* With a policy configured, changing the sandbox mode or backend is rejected until you clear the policy.
* The policy is fixed when a topic is created. After clearing or changing it, existing topics (including ones restored after a daemon restart) keep the old policy; start a new topic.

***

## What works inside the sandbox, and what does not

### `botmux send` still works, credentials stay outside

When the CLI inside the sandbox calls `botmux send` to post text, cards, images or files, it never gets Lark credentials. The request is written to a session-private relay directory and the daemon outside the sandbox sends it. **The Lark App Secret never enters the sandbox.**

Sending somewhere other than the current topic (`--top-level` for the group's top level, `--chat-id` for another group, `--into` for another message's thread) also works, but the daemon re-checks the destination:

* The session's own chat is always allowed;
* Any other chat must be a regular group (not a DM, not an external chat) that the bot is in, and the person who sent this turn's message (or the session owner when there is none) must be a member there and allowed to talk to the bot;
* If any of this cannot be confirmed, the send is refused.

### Fleet commands belong on the host

The sandbox cannot see the supervisor / daemon processes on the host. Running `botmux status / logs / start / stop / restart / start-bot / stop-bot` inside it prints a notice that you are inside a botmux sandbox and asks you to run the command in a host terminal. **The fleet is most likely fine; do not restart it because of this.**

### Common limits (both sandbox modes)

* **No adopt**: a sandbox can only wrap a CLI started from scratch, so `/adopt` is refused. Start a new session instead.
* **No Codex RPC input**: under a sandbox, Codex uses normal terminal input instead of `codexRpcInput`.
* **No dynamic single card**: sandboxed sessions always use the default card mode; see [Cards](/botmux/en/cards.md).
* **Skills are a snapshot taken at spawn**: the enabled managed skills are copied for the session when it starts; after updating a skill, use `/restart` or start a new session. Skills installed as links (`local-link`) or living in a CLI's native skill directory are unavailable under allowlist isolation; `botmux skill show` suggests a copy install instead.
* **Installs inside the sandbox do not reach the host**: if the CLI installs a global skill or package or edits global config, under allowlist isolation it either cannot write or writes to the bot's own directory; under scratch it lands in the throwaway copy. Do installs that should apply globally on the host (Dashboard or a host shell).
* **Sub-agents are sandboxed too**: sub-agents and child processes the CLI spawns inherit the same file and network limits.
* **Zero prompt injection (`promptInjection: "none"`)**: fully supported under allowlist isolation; under scratch, Cursor and Antigravity are not supported (their transcript lands in the throwaway copy and cannot be captured); other CLIs work.

### Supported session backends

| Backend | With a sandbox |
|---|---|
| pty, tmux | Supported |
| zellij, herdr, zmx and other local persistent backends | Cannot set up the same file boundary, so the session **refuses to start**; switch to pty or tmux |
| Riff, remote-runner and other remote backends | The CLI runs remotely, so the local sandbox **has no effect** (the session starts normally and isolation is up to the remote side); combined with `sandboxNetworkPolicy`, though, the session refuses to start |
| mojo | Same as remote backends when it provably runs entirely remote; same as local backends (refuses to start) when it runs on this machine |

***

## Prerequisites in containers / restricted hosts {#linux-namespace}

The Linux sandbox relies on kernel namespaces, which Docker-style containers and hardened hosts often block by default. Check per mode:

| Required capability | Allowlist isolation | scratch | Network policy |
|---|---|---|---|
| bwrap + unprivileged user namespaces + mount / PID namespaces | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| root: kernel overlayfs; non-root: `fuse-overlayfs` + `/dev/fuse` | | ✅ | |
| root (for `scratchStorage: "tmpfs"`; use `"disk"` when non-root) | | ✅ | |
| bwrap with `--add-seccomp-fd` and `--disable-userns`, plus the network tools above | | | ✅ |

Notes:

* **Which bwrap**: the distro binary at `/usr/bin/bwrap` or `/bin/bwrap` is preferred; only when neither exists is a bwrap from `PATH` used, with a one-time warning in the log. Codex installs its own build at `~/.local/bin/bwrap`; when that comes first, sandboxed sessions exit right after launch. Install the distro `bubblewrap` package to fix it.
* **Symlinked system directories**: when a directory such as `/opt` is itself a symlink, the sandbox recreates the same symlink inside and mounts the real path read-only.
* **No downgrade by dropping PID isolation**: other bots' processes on the same host hold plaintext credentials in their environment, which a sandbox without PID isolation could read through `/proc`. So a normal deployment refuses to start when procfs cannot be mounted (only the core-only deployment `BOTMUX_CORE_ONLY=1` allows it).

botmux **never** falls back to running the CLI unsandboxed; it refuses to start the session instead. Common messages:

| Message | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `sandbox requested but could not be established (bwrap missing or setup failed)` | Allowlist isolation could not start |
| `scratch 沙箱没能建立：<reason>。<fix>` (scratch sandbox could not be established) | scratch could not start; the topic names the reason and the fix (missing dependencies, in-memory storage on a non-root daemon, `/dev/fuse` unavailable, a storage setting that no longer matches the session, …). Only in-memory storage lost in a machine reboot needs a new session |
| `[scratch-sandbox] tmpfs upper slot mount failed (non-root host? use scratchStorage "disk")` | In-memory storage on a non-root host |
| `[scratch-sandbox] missing deps (...)` | bubblewrap or fuse-overlayfs is missing and could not be installed automatically (only attempted as root or with passwordless sudo) |
| `bubblewrap cannot establish the required user/mount/PID namespaces` | The host probe failed, typically inside a container |
| `[device-credential-isolation] ... credential-only bubblewrap could not be established` | Machines enrolled with a managed platform and holding a device credential hide credentials with bwrap whether or not the bot has a sandbox; this means bwrap is not usable on that machine |

### Troubleshooting

1. Try bwrap directly:

   ```bash
   bwrap --unshare-user --unshare-pid --bind / / --proc /proc true && echo ok
   ```

   If it fails, namespaces are blocked; fix that first, nothing on the botmux side needs to change.
2. Check whether unprivileged user namespaces are disabled:
   * `cat /proc/sys/user/max_user_namespaces`; `0` means disabled;
   * some distributions also have `/proc/sys/kernel/unprivileged_userns_clone`; `0` means disabled;
   * newer Ubuntu releases may restrict them through AppArmor (`kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns`).
3. Inside a container: the default seccomp profile may block `clone` / `unshare`, and AppArmor / SELinux may block `mount`. Relax this through your container runtime, e.g. `--security-opt seccomp=...`.
4. scratch as non-root: make sure `ls -l /dev/fuse` shows the device and `fuse-overlayfs` is installed; containers need the device passed through (e.g. `--device /dev/fuse`). scratch as root also needs mount capability in a container (e.g. `--cap-add SYS_ADMIN`).
5. Network policy: `bwrap --help` must list `--add-seccomp-fd` and `--disable-userns`; upgrade bubblewrap if it is too old.

Relaxing container isolation weakens the container's own security boundary, so weigh it for your environment.

***

## Three things that are easy to mix up

* **An Oncall directory is not a sandbox**: `/oncall bind <dir>` anchors the bot to a working directory in this group and lets members talk to it directly; it **does not restrict** which files the CLI can read or write. Enable allowlist isolation for that.
* **CLI auto-approval is not "sandbox off"**: the auto-approval flags botmux adds by default (`--dangerously-*`, `--yolo`, etc.; turn them off with `disableCliBypass`) only disable the CLI's **own** approvals / sandbox. The botmux file sandbox wraps the CLI from outside and still applies.
* **`/grant` only grants talk access**: it lets members talk to the bot, but gives no operate rights such as `/cd` or `/restart`, and does not change the sandbox or credentials. See [Permissions](/botmux/en/permissions.md).

***

## Several people on one bot: isolation is stacked

No single layer covers everything; combine them as needed:

| Layer | Isolates | Does not isolate | Where to configure |
|---|---|---|---|
| Session | One CLI process per topic, with its own context and transcript | Files: all sessions see the same host files, and sessions in the same directory see each other's changes; accounts: they share the bot's model account and credentials | Automatic (one session per new topic) |
| Worktree | Each topic edits code in its own git worktree / branch, so topics do not overwrite each other | File access is unchanged; host files outside the worktree are still readable and writable | `/tw`, `/repo wt <repo> [branch]`; see [Slash Commands](/botmux/en/slash-commands.md) |
| File sandbox: off | Nothing | Everything | `sandbox` unset / `false` |
| File sandbox: allowlist isolation | Reads and writes outside the allowlist; credentials, other repositories, other bots' data; the Claude family's and Codex's data directories are split per bot | Writes to allowlisted paths (including the working directory) reach the host directly, and with `workingDir` at its default `~` the whole home directory is allowlisted; other CLIs keep their global host data directory; network is not restricted by default; sessions of the same bot share its model account and CLI data directory | `sandbox: "oncall"` + `sandboxPaths` |
| File sandbox: scratch | Writes (kept in a throwaway copy); botmux's own credentials | Reads: most host files are readable, including other people's tokens; on macOS, cache / preference and system temp dirs still write to the real disk; network is not restricted by default | `sandbox: "scratch"` + `scratchStorage` |
| Per-person tool credentials | lark-cli and other managed tools run with the **current message sender's** own authorization and are refused when that person has not authorized, never borrowing the owner's or anyone else's login | Model account, file access and other unmanaged tools still use the machine / bot identity | `triggerUserAuth`; personal Lark authorization via `/login`, other managed tools reply with an authorization link when needed |
| Model account | Different bots use different model accounts (Claude: `credentialsSourceDir`, sandbox required; Codex: `codexAuthSync: "isolated"`) | Split per bot, not per person: everyone using the same bot shares one model account | The corresponding `bots.json` fields |
| OS user | System-level file permissions, processes and home directories are fully separate | botmux does not provide this layer: every bot and session under one daemon runs as the same system user | Deploy a separate botmux per system user (each with its own `~/.botmux`) |



---
url: /botmux/en/schedule.md
---

# Scheduled Tasks

<video src="../img/video-v5-automation-en.mp4" controls preload="metadata" style="width:100%;border-radius:8px"></video>

Let a bot do work on a schedule: a daily morning report, a service check every 30 minutes, cleaning up a branch once a PR merges. When a task is due, the bot hands your prompt to its AI CLI and posts the result back to Feishu/Lark.

## Quick start

The fastest way is to send this in a group or topic:

```text
/schedule 每日17:50 帮我看看AI圈有什么新闻
```

(`每日17:50` means "every day at 17:50"; the rest is the prompt.) The bot replies with the task ID, next run time and execution position. Use `/schedule list` to view tasks and `/schedule remove <id>` to delete one.

You can also just tell the agent "add a scheduled task to check deployment every day at 18:00". It uses the built-in `botmux-schedule` skill to create it.

## Four ways to create a task

| Way | Good for | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ask the agent | Not remembering syntax | "Summarize alerts every workday at 9" |
| Slash command `/schedule` | Quick task from a chat | `/schedule 工作日每天9:00 检查服务状态` |
| CLI `botmux schedule add` | More options (topics, model, until-done…) | `botmux schedule add "every 2h" "check the build"` |
| Dashboard **Scheduled Tasks** page | Visual editing, run logs, preconditions, calendars | Click **New Task** |

When you run `botmux schedule add` inside a bot session, the chat is inferred. Outside a session, add `--chat-id <chat ID>`.

<img src="/img/schedule-dashboard-list.png" alt="Dashboard scheduled task list: each task shows its type, target chat, execution position and next run, with Run Now, Enable, Edit and Delete buttons" />

## Writing the schedule

**The `/schedule` slash command only understands Chinese phrases** (schedule first, then the prompt):

| Phrase | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `每日17:50` / `每天9点` / `每天9点30分` | Every day at a time |
| `工作日每天9:00` / `每个工作日9:00` | Monday to Friday (ignores public holidays; use a [work calendar](#work-calendars) for those) |
| `每周一10:00` | Every week on a day (一 = Monday … 日 = Sunday) |
| `每月1号9:00` | Every month on a day |
| `每小时` / `每2小时` | Every hour / every N hours, on the hour |
| `每30分钟` | Every N minutes, clock-aligned |
| `30分钟后` / `2小时后` / `明天9:00` | Once: in 30 minutes / in 2 hours / tomorrow at 9:00 |

**The CLI and Dashboard accept more formats:**

```bash
botmux schedule add "每日9:00" "good morning"          # all Chinese phrases above work
botmux schedule add "every 2h" "check the services"    # fixed interval
botmux schedule add "30m" "remind me to drink water"   # once, 30 minutes from now
botmux schedule add "0 9 * * *" "good morning"         # 5-field cron
botmux schedule add "2026-12-01T10:00" "release reminder"  # once at a time
```

### Time zone

Cron and phrases like "every day at 9" fire, "tomorrow 9:00" is parsed, and times on cards and in the Dashboard are shown, all in one time zone. By default it follows the host.

If the server and you are in different time zones (say the host is overseas and you're in Beijing), pick `Asia/Shanghai` under Dashboard "General → Scheduled tasks → Timezone" (stored as `scheduleTimeZone` in `config.json`), or set the environment variable `BOTMUX_SCHEDULE_TIMEZONE`. The environment variable wins. See [Global Settings: Scheduled task timezone](/botmux/en/global-settings.md#scheduled-task-timezone).

The exception is an explicit date-time: `2026-12-01T10:00` without an offset is read in the host time zone, not this setting. To pin a zone, include the offset, e.g. `2026-12-01T10:00+08:00`.

## Where results go: execution position

**By default a task runs at the chat's top level**, even if you created it inside a topic. It does not automatically return to that topic. To change that, pick one of these:

| Execution position | Effect | How to set |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chat top level (default) | Follows the bot / chat session mode; top-level tasks in one chat share the chat-level session | Default; CLI `--top-level` |
| A specific topic | Every run goes to one existing topic and continues its context | CLI `--topic` (uses the current topic inside a topic session, or `--root-msg-id <om_...>`) |
| New topic each run | Each run opens a fresh topic with its own session; good for daily reports | Prefix the prompt with `新话题`; CLI `--new-topic` |
| Dedicated task topic | The task owns one topic and keeps continuing in it; tasks don't mix | Prefix the prompt with `独立话题` or `专属话题` |

The Dashboard **Execution position** dropdown changes it directly. An admin can also send `/dashboard schedules` to get a DM card; the task detail view there can pause, resume or switch the execution position.

### New topic each run

```bash
# Slash command: prefix the prompt with 新话题 ("new topic")
/schedule 每日17:30 新话题 生成今天的群讨论日报

# CLI
botmux schedule add "每日17:30" "write the daily report" --new-topic
```

The first message of the new topic is the "task started" notice by default. Set your own title with `--topic-title` (up to 200 characters). Non-silent tasks can use placeholders:

| Placeholder | Becomes |
| --- | --- |
| `{{date}}` | The run's date in the schedule time zone, e.g. `2026-11-05` |
| `{{date:-1d}}` / `{{date:+2d}}` | A date some days before / after |
| `{{owner}}` | An @mention of the task creator (only for tasks with a recorded creator) |

```bash
botmux schedule add "每日9:00" "summarize yesterday's alerts" --new-topic --topic-title "{{date:-1d}} alert report {{owner}}"
```

Silent tasks only support fixed titles; templates are rejected on save.

### Dedicated task topic

* Every run of the same task lands in **the same topic**, so context carries over.
* Different tasks in the same chat each get their own topic, so a health check and a daily report never share a session.
* The topic is **created on the first run**: a non-silent task posts a "task started" message to start the topic; a silent task waits until the bot first speaks with `botmux send`.
* Only single-chat tasks are supported.

```text
/schedule 每日18:00 独立话题 汇总今天的服务巡检结果
/schedule 每个工作日9:00 静默 专属话题 生成晨报，有异常才说话
```

Keywords such as `静默` (silent) and `独立话题` can be combined in any order.

### Follow the active topic

A fixed-topic task has a weakness: when the topic closes and people move elsewhere, reminders land where nobody looks. With `--follow-active`, the task picks a target again on every run:

```bash
# Created inside a topic session: the starting point is the current topic
botmux schedule add "every 30m" "check service status, alert only on failure" --follow-active

# Or give the starting point explicitly
botmux schedule add "每日9:00" "stand-up reminder" --follow-active --root-msg-id om_xxx
```

Each run checks, in order:

1. The last topic is still open and a human has spoken in it → post there again.
2. Otherwise → post to the topic in this chat where **a human spoke most recently**, and remember it (bot replies don't count). The task then runs in that existing session, so its own `--workdir` doesn't apply.
3. No open topic with human messages, but the last topic is still open → stay put.
4. Nothing is open → open a new top-level topic and remember it.

If session records can't be read (for example the database is temporarily unavailable), the target doesn't move. `--follow-active` can't be combined with `--top-level` / `--new-topic`. In `schedule list` these tasks are marked `↷跟随活跃话题`.

## Silent mode

For checks that should stay quiet unless something is wrong:

```text
/schedule 每30分钟 静默 检查服务，挂了才报警
```

On the CLI use `--silent`. A silent task posts no "task started" notice; the model decides whether to send anything with `botmux send`. With a new topic, the topic is only created when there's something to say.

## Managing tasks

In a chat:

```text
/schedule list               # list tasks (also 列表)
/schedule remove <id>        # delete (also 删除)
/schedule disable <id>       # pause (also 禁用)
/schedule enable <id>        # resume (also 启用)
/schedule run <id>           # run once now (also 执行)
```

CLI:

```bash
botmux schedule list
botmux schedule pause <id>
botmux schedule resume <id>
botmux schedule run <id>
botmux schedule remove <id>
```

In a chat, `/schedule list` shows each task's run-as identity (`runAs`). A task with no usable identity is flagged, because tools that need a user identity will fail closed. See [Run-as identity](#run-as-identity-and-permissions).

### Edit the frequency, prompt or calendar in place

No need to delete and recreate — use `update`:

```bash
botmux schedule update <id> --schedule "every 4h"         # change the frequency; same syntax as schedule add
botmux schedule update <id> --prompt-file report-prompt.md
# Short prompts can be passed inline (--prompt or --prompt-file, not both)
botmux schedule update <id> --prompt "new full prompt"
# Fields can be combined
botmux schedule update <id> --schedule "0 9 * * 1-5" --prompt-file report-prompt.md
```

`--schedule` accepts everything `schedule add` does (`每日17:50`, `every 2h`, 5-field cron, …); an expression it can't read is rejected with examples and the task is left alone. After a frequency change the next run is recomputed from now under the new rule — nothing is re-run or fired immediately — and the command prints the new rule and the next run time. A paused task stays paused. The frequency can't be changed while a run is in progress (you'll be asked to wait for it to finish), and a one-shot time can't be in the past.

The task ID, silent setting, execution position, Bash precondition, work calendar, creator identity, enabled state and run history are kept. A run already in progress keeps the old configuration; the next run uses the new one. Permissions match the Dashboard edit: whoever can change the prompt can change the frequency, and delegated tasks still need a new authorization. See `botmux schedule update --help` for every field.

## Run logs and multiple groups (Dashboard) {#logs-and-multi-chat}

Like the [Bash precondition](#bash-precondition), these two are only available on the Dashboard's **Scheduled Tasks** page.

**Run logs**: every row in the task list has a **Run logs** button. It shows recent runs: whether each one was submitted to the model, skipped because the precondition failed, or failed to schedule, plus the trigger (scheduler / Dashboard run now), start and end times and the precondition result. The log only covers the precondition check and the submission to the model; it does not include model output, terminal output or message delivery. Only runs recorded after the upgrade are shown, and viewing the log never triggers or changes the task.

**One task, several groups**: when creating or editing a task, **Bound groups** accepts several groups, up to 5.

* Each group calls the model independently, and a failure in one group doesn't stop the others; model usage grows with the number of groups.
* The Bash precondition runs once per schedule, and its result applies to every group.
* With the execution position set to **Dedicated topic for this task** or to a specific existing topic, only one group can be bound.

## Per-task model

A high-frequency sentinel is fine on a cheap model; a daily deep review deserves the strongest one. `--model` / `--reasoning-effort` apply to this task only and leave the bot config alone:

```bash
# High-frequency sentinel: cheap model, low effort
botmux schedule add "every 30m" "check service status, alert only on failure" \
  --silent --model gpt-5.2 --reasoning-effort low

# Once-a-day deep task
botmux schedule add "每日9:00" "review every PR merged to master yesterday" \
  --new-topic --model gpt-5.6-sol --reasoning-effort ultra
```

The Dashboard form has **Model** and **Reasoning effort** fields too; leave them empty to follow the bot config.

**Note: only the run that starts a new session can switch models.** The model is a launch argument of the CLI process and can't change once it's running:

| Execution position | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| New topic each run | Every run starts a new session, so the model applies **every time** |
| Dedicated task topic / specific topic / chat top level | Only the run that creates the session applies it; later runs keep the session's original model |

Reasoning effort can be `low` / `medium` / `high` / `xhigh` / `max` / `ultra`; which levels work depends on the model. Per-task models are supported on Codex, Codex App, Claude Code, Grok, TRAE (TraeX), Kimi, ZCode and Remote Runner. If at run time the bot has switched to a CLI without support, or the model no longer supports the level, that setting is dropped with a warning and the task runs anyway; it is never skipped for this reason.

## Until done: stateful follow-up tasks

For jobs like "switch back to main once the PR merges" or "delete the backup after Oct 30", use `--until-done`. The task keeps running on schedule until the session running it confirms the work is done and marks it complete.

```bash
# Check daily at 10:07, until Nov 20 at the latest
botmux schedule add "7 10 * * *" "After PR #123 merges, switch the cluster back to upstream and clean up the temporary worktree" \
  --until-done --deadline 2026-11-20 --silent

# Do it after a date; if not done, retry every 6 hours (one-shot default is 1 day)
botmux schedule add "2026-10-30T10:00" "Delete the pre-upgrade backup directory" --until-done --retry-every 6h

# From the running session, once the work is done (mark first, then send the final reply)
botmux schedule done self --note "Back on upstream; worktree cleaned up"
```

`--deadline` accepts a date, `7d`, `明天18:00` (tomorrow 18:00) and similar.

| Situation | Normal task | `--until-done` task |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Run succeeds | One-shot task is disabled | Stays on; one-shot task runs again after `--retry-every` |
| Run fails / interrupted by a daemon restart | One-shot task is disabled | Stays on; one-shot task retries within 1 hour, recurring task waits for the next run |
| Missed run (daemon down, etc.) | Skips to the next one | Catches up once right away, then resumes its rhythm |
| `--deadline` reached | — | One final closing run, then closes as "expired"; a failed closing run retries every 60 minutes, up to 3 times |
| `botmux schedule done` | N/A | Closes as "completed" with the result note |

Each run gets a footer appended to the prompt with the run number, deadline and how to mark completion, so your prompt only needs to say what to wait for and what to do. Completed or expired tasks can't be resumed; create a new one. Tasks created through cross-bot delegation don't support `--until-done` yet.

**Run ledger**: every task records runs, skips, failures and misses. `botmux schedule list` shows two extra lines per task:

```text
   状态: 直到完成 · 进行中 · 已执行 3 次 · 截止 2026/11/20 00:00:00
   账本: 执行 3 · 跳过 0 · 失败 1 · 错过 1（最近 2026/10/26 10:07:00）
```

(Status: until-done · in progress · ran 3 times · deadline …; Ledger: ran 3 · skipped 0 · failed 1 · missed 1.)

**Failure notifications**:

* `--notify failing,expired`: @mentions the creator in the topic where the task was created (or the target chat if there is none). `failing` fires after 3 failures in a row (once per streak); `expired` fires when the task closes at its deadline. Off by default.
* Admin fallback: whether or not `--notify` is set, any task that fails 3 times in a row DMs one admin once; it resets after a successful run.

## Bash precondition

To check something first and call the model only when a condition holds (saving cost and noise), turn on **Enable Bash precondition** when creating or editing a task in the Dashboard.

<img src="/img/schedule-bash-precondition.jpg" alt="Bash precondition section of the Dashboard task form: enable switch, configuration source (enter Bash directly / Bash file path) and script box" width="520" />

**There is one rule**: the script must exit with `0` and its stdout, trimmed, must be **exactly `1`** for the model to be called. Output `0`, anything else, empty output or an error skips this run.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Replace with what you actually need to check on the daemon host
if test -f /srv/my-service/ready.flag; then
  printf '1\n'
else
  printf '0\n'
fi
```

To give this model call extra context, write to file descriptor 3 (FD 3); it is appended to the prompt:

```bash
printf '1\n'
cat >&3 <<'PROMPT'
The deployment check passed. Continue the analysis with this in mind.
PROMPT
```

FD 3 content is sent to the model and may end up in the session log. Never print secrets or tokens.

**Two ways to configure it:**

* **Enter Bash directly**: the script is stored with the task.
* **Bash file path**: the file must live in the trusted directory the Dashboard shows, `<dataDir>/schedule-preconditions/trusted-files/` on the daemon host. Enter the **full absolute path**. Relative paths, `~`, the directory itself, files outside it and paths containing symlinks are rejected. The file is re-read on every test and run, so editing it doesn't require re-saving the task.

Then click **Test precondition**. It really runs the current (unsaved) form content on the daemon host and shows passed, not passed, or an error code. Testing doesn't save, doesn't call the model and doesn't count as a run, but the script's own side effects (writing files, network calls) do happen.

Turning the switch off only pauses the precondition; the task still runs and the script is kept. Clear the script or path and save to remove it.

> File paths saved outside the trusted directory before an upgrade are kept, but while enabled both testing and scheduled runs refuse them (no model call). Move the file into the trusted directory yourself, update the full path, test, then save.

## Work calendars

"Workdays at 9" means Monday to Friday, which breaks around public holidays and make-up workdays. Bind a work calendar and the scheduler filters runs by it:

```bash
botmux schedule add "0 9 * * *" "write the daily report" --calendar cn   # statutory workdays only
botmux schedule calendars                                                # list available calendars
```

> To run on Chinese statutory workdays, use **a daily cron plus the calendar** (e.g. `0 9 * * *`). `0 9 * * 1-5` never fires on weekends, so a calendar can't create the weekend make-up workday for it.

### Built-in China statutory calendar

ID `cn`, shown as "China Statutory Work Calendar", time zone `Asia/Shanghai`, including holidays and weekend make-up workdays. **Currently verified for 2026-01-01 to 2026-12-31**, based on the [State Council General Office notice on 2026 holidays](https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/202511/content_7047091.htm) (Guobanfa Mingdian \[2025] No. 7). `schedule calendars` prints the source details.

It represents the nationwide holiday arrangement, not every organization's actual shifts; local holidays, company rosters, Hong Kong/Macao/Taiwan and other countries are out of scope. Dates outside coverage (such as the not-yet-verified 2027) are never guessed: the task stops running automatically and records `calendar_out_of_coverage`. Upgrade to a release with next year's data before the year ends.

### Custom calendars

For company rosters and the like, add your own calendar to the bot. The default path is `~/.botmux/bots/<appId>/work-calendars.json` (next to that bot's `schedules.json`); each bot's calendars are separate. Changes are picked up on the next check without a restart.

The following is **made-up demo data**:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "calendars": {
    "demo": {
      "timeZone": "Asia/Shanghai",
      "displayNames": { "zh": "演示工作日历", "en": "Demo Work Calendar" },
      "coverage": { "start": "2027-12-30", "end": "2028-12-31" },
      "workWeek": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5],
      "restDates": ["2028-01-04"],
      "workDates": ["2028-01-01", "2028-01-08"]
    }
  }
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `version` | File format version, currently `1` |
| `calendars` | Calendar name → definition; names are 1–64 letters, digits, `_` or `-`, starting with a letter or digit |
| `displayNames` | Optional Chinese/English display names; the calendar ID is shown if omitted |
| `timeZone` | IANA time zone used to decide "which day it is" |
| `coverage.start/end` | Inclusive date range the data is confirmed for, `YYYY-MM-DD` |
| `workWeek` | Default working weekdays; `0` is Sunday, `1` is Monday, … |
| `restDates` | Extra days off |
| `workDates` | Extra workdays (e.g. weekend make-up days) |

Everything except `displayNames` is required. Duplicate dates, a day listed as both rest and work, an invalid time zone or a reversed range invalidate that definition. The file is limited to 1 MiB. One bad definition doesn't affect the others, but a malformed file stops every task bound to it from running automatically. `cn` is reserved and can't be overridden locally.

### Bind, change and unbind

```bash
botmux schedule add "0 9 * * *" "write the daily report" --calendar cn
botmux schedule update <task-id> --calendar cn                # rebind
botmux schedule update <task-id> --calendar-day-type restday  # run on rest days only (default: workday)
botmux schedule update <task-id> --calendar none              # unbind
```

In the Dashboard form, pick a calendar under **Custom Work Calendar**, choose **Workdays only** or **Rest days only** under **Run on**, or choose **No calendar filter** to unbind. Task rows show the **Next calendar-eligible trigger** and the reason.

### How calendars affect runs

| Trigger | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Automatic cron / interval | Checks the calendar when due; if the day type doesn't match, skips and waits for the next run, with no catch-up |
| One-shot task | Can't be bound to a calendar |
| Dashboard **Run Now** / `schedule run` | Manual runs bypass the calendar (preconditions still apply) |

* The calendar check happens before the precondition, the model call and topic creation. A skip is recorded as a skip, not a failure, and doesn't use up repeat counts.
* If the calendar is missing, broken or out of coverage, the task doesn't run and the reason is recorded, but the task isn't disabled; once the data is fixed, later runs proceed. A calendar read failure counts as one failure, and 3 in a row trigger failure notifications.
* A paused task can't `schedule run`; resume it first. Pausing cancels pending manual run requests.

Common reason codes: `work_date` / `work_week` allow the run, `rest_date` / `rest_week` skip it; `calendar_missing` (no such calendar), `calendar_invalid` (bad format), `calendar_out_of_coverage` (outside the covered dates).

If your own job script also hard-codes "Monday to Friday only", remove that, or it will still skip weekend make-up workdays the calendar allows.

## Run-as identity and permissions

When a task runs, whose identity is used for per-user tools like `lark-cli --as user` and `bytedcli`? The rule:

1. Someone claimed it → the claimant;
2. Otherwise → the creator (recorded automatically when a human creates the task in Feishu/Lark).

Every run re-checks that this person can still operate the bot.

| Where the task was created | Recorded creator |
| --- | --- |
| A human in Feishu/Lark via `/schedule` or the agent | The message sender |
| Dashboard through platform Feishu login | The signed-in person (must be able to operate the bot; otherwise the bot owner is recorded) |
| Dashboard local token link | The bot owner |
| Host terminal `botmux schedule add` | No person; use `--run-as <ou_... or Feishu email>` to set the run-as identity, who must be able to operate the bot |

`--run-as` only works from the host terminal; tasks created inside a session always run as the current requester.

### Claim card

If the bot has user identity auth on (`triggerUserAuth` in `bots.json`) and a task has no usable identity (no recorded creator, or the creator/claimant lost access), the bot posts a claim card in the task's chat (or topic) when it fires, instead of letting the task fail silently:

<img src="/img/schedule-identity-claim-card.jpg" alt="Four states of the scheduled-task claim card: pending (no creator), pending (creator lost access), claimed, and no longer needs a claim" />

* Click **Claim — run it as me**: every later run uses your identity. The identity comes from the clicker Feishu reports, so it can't be forged.
* After a claim you can use **Claim it for me instead** or **Run again**.
* Only members who can operate the bot can click. Each task has one card, refreshed in place on later runs.

(The screenshot shows the Chinese UI.)

### Who can manage tasks

* Creating, running, pausing, resuming, deleting and updating tasks are all judged by whether **the human sender of the current turn** is an operator of this bot. Bot messages, old messages and automatic continuations can't stand in for a human.
* A task's own run can stop itself with `botmux schedule pause self` / `remove self` (re-checking each time that the creator is still an admin and still in the chat; host-terminal tasks with no creator can do this too). It can only manage this one task: no prompt changes, no resume, no forced runs.
* To "send the final result, then delete myself", use one command instead of two steps:

```bash
botmux send --response-kind final --schedule-remove-self --no-mention "Task complete"
```

BotMux first confirms the result was delivered, then deletes the current task. If `scheduleSelfCleanup.removed` in the result is `false`, retry the same command; the message won't be sent twice.

The authoritative task records live in a host-side SQLite database; `schedules.json` is only a rebuildable copy, and hand-adding records there won't make a task run. So every write goes to the owning bot's daemon. If the daemon is unavailable the command fails loudly, instead of editing only the JSON and leaving a task that never runs.

## Advanced: cross-bot delegated creation

When a human explicitly asks Bot A, in the current turn, to have Bot B create a scheduled task, A must request the capability on the managed dispatch:

```bash
botmux dispatch --bot-app cli_target --title "Polling task" --brief "Create and maintain the poll" \
  --delegate schedule:create
```

The host must also turn it on in `~/.botmux/config.json` (off by default):

```json
{
  "scheduleDelegation": {
    "createEnabled": true,
    "runEnabled": true,
    "maxTasksPerTurn": 64,
    "runScopes": ["bytedcli"],
    "selfManageEnabled": true
  }
}
```

| Setting | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `createEnabled` | Allow new delegations; off by default. Turning it off stops new ones, and tasks created via `botGrants` also stop running |
| `runEnabled` | Whether already delegated tasks keep running; on if omitted. The emergency stop |
| `maxTasksPerTurn` | Max tasks per dispatch turn; default 64, max 1024 |
| `runScopes` | Personal credentials a delegated task may reuse on later runs; currently only `bytedcli`; empty by default |
| `selfManageEnabled` | Whether delegated tasks may pause/remove themselves from their own runs; off by default |
| `defaultOnDispatchFromBotAppIds` | Managed dispatches from these source bots request `schedule:create` by default; opt out per dispatch with `--no-delegate schedule:create` |
| `botGrants` | Bot scheduling grants: pre-authorize by "source bot + target bots + chats", so dispatches not triggered by an admin can still create tasks on behalf of a "controller admin"; requires `createEnabled` |

These are also editable in the Dashboard under **Global Settings → Experimental** (**Cross-bot delegated scheduled tasks**, **Delegated task self-management**, **Bot scheduling grants**).

With `runScopes`, both the source and target bots must enable `triggerUserAuth`, and the target bot must route both `lark-cli` and `bytedcli` through identity isolation:

```json
"triggerUserAuth": {
  "enabled": true,
  "tools": ["lark-cli", "bytedcli"]
}
```

Limits: delegation is single-hop and bound to the target bot's current dispatch turn; it expires when the turn ends. Tasks can only land at the top level of the original dispatch chat or in the current topic; `--new-topic`, `--follow-active`, multiple chats and re-delegation aren't supported. Retrying the same request returns the original task instead of creating a duplicate.



---
url: /botmux/en/session-model.md
---

# Session & Topic Model

In botmux, **a session = one running AI coding CLI process (such as Claude Code or Codex) + its context**. Every message you send lands in some session.

Questions like "why does every @ feel like starting over" or "why can't a new group see earlier chat" all come down to which session a message landed in. This page explains that, and how to start, continue, and recover sessions.

## At a glance: which session does a message go to

| Where you chat | How sessions are split by default | How to change it |
|----------------|-----------------------------------|------------------|
| **Topic group** | One session per topic; topics don't affect each other | Nothing to set up; recommended |
| **Regular group** | Top-level messages that @ the bot share one session; each topic opened in the group gets its own session | `/reply-mode`, see "Regular groups" below |
| **Direct message** | Your whole DM with the bot is one continuous session | `/reply-mode`, see "Direct messages" below |
| **Session group created with `/g`** | The whole group is one session | See [One-step session groups](/botmux/en/group.md) |
| **On-call group** | Bound to one project directory; anyone in the group can @ the bot and ask | See [On-Call Mode](/botmux/en/oncall.md) |

> Sessions are **per bot**. If you @ two bots in the same topic, that's two independent sessions that don't share context.

## Topic groups

Each new topic starts a new session; replying inside a topic continues that session. Topics are fully isolated, which makes them good for running several tasks in parallel.

## Regular groups

How a regular group splits sessions depends on its "reply mode". Each bot has a default, and a single group can override it with `/reply-mode`:

| Mode | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `chat-topic` (default) | Top-level @s all go into one session; each topic opened in the group is its own session |
| `chat` | The whole group is one session; messages in topics are folded in too |
| `new-topic` | Every @ opens a new topic and a new session |
| `topic` (also `shared`) | Replies show up in topics, but all topics share one session |

* See the current mode: `/reply-mode`; go back to the bot default: `/reply-mode inherit`.
* Change the bot default in Dashboard "Bot config", or set `regularGroupReplyMode` in `bots.json` (see [bots.json](/botmux/en/bots-json.md)).

**To open a dedicated topic for a task in a regular group**, use `/t`:

```text
Fix login page bug /t /repo my-app The login button does nothing, please take a look
```

* Text before `/t` is the topic title. After it you can add `/repo` (pick a repository), `/model` (pick a model), and the first task.
* Bare `/t` just sets up the topic. If a repository must be picked, a repo picker card appears; otherwise it waits for your next task or `/repo` in the topic, without starting an empty session.
* `/th` opens a topic in the current group session's working directory; `/tw` creates a worktree first, then opens the topic.
* Full syntax is in [Slash Commands](/botmux/en/slash-commands.md).

> When "show a status card while a task runs" is off, `/t <text>` still posts a visible reply first so Lark expands the topic right away; reactions are only progress hints.

## Direct messages

By default your whole DM is one continuous session, so everything builds on earlier context. Each person's DM with the bot is separate. To change this:

| Command | Effect |
|---------|--------|
| `/reply-mode chat` (default) | The whole DM is one continuous session |
| `/reply-mode topic` | Each top-level DM message starts its own session; replying in that message's thread continues that session |
| `/reply-mode group` | Each top-level DM message creates a dedicated "you + bot" group and runs the session there; see [One-step session groups](/botmux/en/group.md) |

The DM mode applies to **all DMs** with that bot, and maps to `p2pMode` in `bots.json`.

## Common tasks: start, continue, recover

| You want to | Do this |
|-------------|---------|
| Continue where you left off | Reply in the **same topic** (topic group), or go back to the same group / DM |
| Start a new session | Post a new topic in a topic group; use `/t` in a regular group |
| Work on something else in parallel with the current context | `/fork <task>` opens a forked topic that inherits the full context |
| Find topics still open in this group | `/sessions`, then click "back to topic" to jump there |
| End a session | `/close`. The next message starts a new session |
| Bring back a closed session | Click "▶️ Resume session" on the close card, or send `/resume` |

![/sessions card: lists the topic sessions still open in this group](/img/sessions-command-card.png)

## A session's lifecycle

| Stage | What's happening |
|-------|------------------|
| Starting | The first message arrived and the bot is launching the CLI |
| Working | The CLI is thinking and running; the status card refreshes live |
| Awaiting input | This turn is done; you can send the next message |
| Dormant | After a long idle period, or when too many sessions are live, the CLI process exits to free memory. The topic stays, and the next message restores the context automatically |
| Closed | Someone sent `/close` or clicked the close button. A new message starts a new session; resume it to continue the old one |

Each turn gets a new status card, and the previous card freezes in its final state so you can look back. Card colors and buttons are in [Live Streaming Cards](/botmux/en/cards.md); what triggers dormancy and whether a daemon restart loses context are in the [FAQ](/botmux/en/faq.md).

## The four names of a session

"I renamed it, so why didn't Lark change?" Because a session has four separate names:

| Name | Where it shows | How to change it |
|------|----------------|------------------|
